title: Why you pant when you run: how blood and breath deliver oxygen to every cell

summary.text: Run up a flight of stairs and two things happen that you did not ask for. You start to pant, and your heart starts to thump. Nobody gave either of them an order. In this unit you count your pulse and your breaths in five situations, and find that they rise and fall together. Then you follow the oxygen from your nose, through very thin walls in the lungs, into red blood cells, and out to every cell in your body.
summary.art: A child at the top of a staircase with one hand on her chest and one on her wrist, and a faint drawing over her body of air going in, red blood moving round, and tiny cells receiving oxygen.

intro.hook: Sit still and count how many times you breathe in one minute. Then count how many times your heart beats. Which number is bigger, and by how much?
intro.text: Most people find that their heart beats about four times for every breath. Now jump on the spot for one minute and count both again. Both numbers go up, and both go up together. Why would a heart and a pair of lungs, so far apart, speed up at the same moment?
intro.art: A child sitting on a floor mat with two fingers on her wrist, and a parent beside her holding a phone stopwatch, with a small label that says count for 15 seconds.

outcomes: I can find my pulse, count my breaths, and say what is a usual rate for a child at rest.
I can plan a fair test of what changes pulse and breathing rate, and show the results on a line graph.
I can explain that blood carries oxygen from the lungs and food from the gut to every cell, and carries carbon dioxide back.
I can name what blood is made of, and say what red blood cells and haemoglobin do.
I can explain why the heart has two sides, one sending blood to the lungs and one sending it to the body.
I can explain why lungs and capillaries are built so thin and so wide, using the idea of surface area.
I can explain why pulse and breathing rate rise together, and what tells the body to do it.
I can say how blood moves to where it is needed most, and why cold fingers go pale.

terms.meaning: The small push you can feel in an artery each time the heart beats. You feel it best on the inside of your wrist.
terms.example: Two fingers on your wrist feel about 85 pushes in one minute when you sit still.
terms.art: Two fingers resting on the inside of a child's wrist, with small waves drawn under the skin.

terms.meaning: How many times your heart beats in one minute. It is the same number as your pulse rate.
terms.example: A child sitting still has a heart rate of about 70 to 110 beats per minute.
terms.art: A heart with the number 85 beside it and a label that says beats in one minute.

terms.meaning: How many breaths you take in one minute. One breath is one time in and one time out.
terms.example: A child sitting still takes about 18 to 25 breaths in one minute.
terms.art: A child's chest rising and falling, with the numbers 1, 2, 3 above each breath.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air. Every cell in your body uses oxygen to get energy out of food. Air is about one fifth oxygen.
terms.example: The oxygen in your last breath came from the air, and some of it is already in your blood.
terms.art: Air drawn as small blue dots going into a child's nose, with a few of them coloured red inside the chest.

terms.meaning: A gas that cells make when they use food for energy. Blood carries it back to the lungs and you breathe it out.
terms.example: Your breath turns limewater milky because it carries carbon dioxide.
terms.art: Small grey dots leaving a child's open mouth, with an arrow from the body to the air.

terms.meaning: A tiny, round, flat cell in your blood that carries oxygen. It is shaped like a doughnut with a dent instead of a hole.
terms.example: A speck of blood the size of a pinhead holds about 5 million red blood cells.
terms.art: Many red doughnut-shaped cells with dents in the middle, floating in a pale yellow liquid.

terms.meaning: A red protein inside red blood cells. It holds oxygen, and it has iron in it. It is the reason blood is red.
terms.example: One red blood cell holds about 270 million haemoglobin molecules.
terms.art: A red blood cell cut in half, packed with small red shapes, each holding blue oxygen dots.

terms.meaning: The pale yellow liquid part of blood. It carries blood cells, food, salts and waste.
terms.example: A little more than half of your blood is plasma, and most of it is water.
terms.art: A test tube of blood that has settled into a yellow top layer and a red bottom layer.

terms.meaning: A tiny piece of a cell that helps blood to clot. When you get a cut, platelets stick together and plug the hole.
terms.example: A scab starts with platelets gathering at a cut.
terms.art: A cut on a knee with small platelets clumping at the edge and a net of threads over them.

terms.meaning: A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. It has a thick, stretchy wall, and you can feel your pulse in one.
terms.example: The pulse in your wrist is a push of blood going along an artery.
terms.art: A heart with a thick red tube leaving it and a hand feeling the tube at the wrist.

terms.meaning: A blood vessel that carries blood back to the heart. It has a thinner wall and small flaps inside that stop blood from slipping backwards.
terms.example: The bluish lines on the back of your hand are veins.
terms.art: The back of a hand with veins drawn, and a cut-away of one vein showing small flaps.

terms.meaning: The thinnest blood vessel. Its wall is only one cell thick, so oxygen and food can pass through it to the cells outside.
terms.example: Red blood cells squeeze through a capillary in a single line.
terms.art: A very thin tube with red blood cells passing one by one, and blue dots leaving through the wall.

terms.meaning: A tiny air bag at the end of the airways in your lungs. The plural is alveoli. Oxygen passes through its wall into the blood.
terms.example: An adult has several hundred million alveoli, packed like bunches of grapes.
terms.art: A bunch of tiny air sacs like grapes on a stalk, each wrapped in a net of thin red capillaries.

terms.meaning: The swap in the lungs. Oxygen goes from the air into the blood, and carbon dioxide goes from the blood into the air.
terms.example: Your breath out has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than the air you breathed in.
terms.art: One alveolus with blue arrows going into a capillary and grey arrows coming out.

terms.meaning: Blood goes through the heart twice on one full trip round the body. The right side sends it to the lungs, and the left side sends it to the body.
terms.example: A drop of blood goes to the lungs, comes back to the heart, and then goes out to your toes.
terms.art: A figure of eight with the heart in the middle, one loop to the lungs and one loop to the body.

terms.meaning: Having too few red blood cells, or too little haemoglobin. The body gets less oxygen, so a person feels tired and breathless.
terms.example: Not eating enough iron-rich food, such as ragi, dal and green leaves, is one cause of anaemia.
terms.art: A tired child sitting on a step with a pale face, next to a plate of ragi roti, dal and spinach.

explanations.concept: Pulse and breathing rate: two numbers you can count
explanations.definition: Your pulse rate is the number of heartbeats in one minute. Your breathing rate is the number of breaths in one minute. Both change all day.
explanations.description: Press two fingers, not your thumb, on the inside of your wrist and you feel a small push again and again. Each push is one heartbeat travelling along an artery. Count the pushes for 15 seconds and multiply by 4, and you have your pulse rate. To count breaths, watch a chest or a belly rise and fall for 15 seconds, and multiply by 4. A child of 6 to 10 sitting still has a pulse rate of about 70 to 110 beats per minute and a breathing rate of about 18 to 25 breaths per minute. A grown-up at rest has a slower pulse and slower breathing. A newborn baby has a much faster pulse and breathing. Heart rate and breathing rate are not fixed numbers. They are answers that your body gives, moment by moment, to the question: how much is being asked of me right now?
examples: A child lying down has a lower pulse than the same child standing up.
After 30 step-ups, a child's pulse can double, and then falls back over a few minutes.
A sleeping person has one of the slowest pulses of the day.
explanations.art: A child's wrist with two fingers on it, and a chest with a hand on it, each with a stopwatch and the number of counts written beside it.

explanations.concept: Why cells need oxygen: getting energy out of food
explanations.definition: Every cell uses oxygen to get energy out of food. The cell makes carbon dioxide and water as waste.
explanations.description: Food holds energy, but a cell cannot use it straight away. Inside the cell, tiny parts called mitochondria take sugar from your food and oxygen from the air. They use the two together to release energy, and they leave carbon dioxide and water behind. This is called cellular respiration. It is slow burning without a flame. Your muscles, your brain and your heart are all busy cells, so all of them need oxygen all the time. The brain is only a small part of your weight, but it uses about one fifth of your oxygen. The food comes from the gut, and the oxygen comes from the lungs. The blood is the delivery system that brings both to every cell, and takes the carbon dioxide away.
examples: A cell in a leg muscle needs more oxygen when you run, because it is releasing energy faster.
Brain cells keep using oxygen even when you sit and think, or when you sleep.
The carbon dioxide in your breath is made from the carbon in the food you ate.
explanations.art: A single cell with a sugar cube going in on one side, oxygen going in on the other, and arrows for carbon dioxide and water going out, with a lightning bolt of energy in the middle.

explanations.concept: Gas exchange: why lungs are so thin and so wide
explanations.definition: Gas exchange is the swap in the lungs. Oxygen goes from the air into the blood, and carbon dioxide goes the other way.
explanations.description: Air travels down your windpipe and splits into narrower and narrower tubes, like the branches of a tree. At the end of each twig is a tiny air bag called an alveolus. An adult has several hundred million of them. Each alveolus is wrapped in a net of capillaries, and the wall between air and blood is only about half a thousandth of a millimetre thick. Oxygen is more crowded in the air in the alveolus than in the blood that arrives, so oxygen drifts into the blood. Carbon dioxide is more crowded in the blood, so it drifts out into the air. This drifting needs no push. It is called diffusion, and it works well only when the wall is very thin and the surface is very large. If you could spread out all the alveoli flat, the surface would be somewhere between 50 and 100 square metres in an adult. Scientists give a range because it is hard to measure, and a child's lungs are smaller. Air you breathe out still holds about 16 out of every 100 parts oxygen, which is why mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing works.
examples: Air in is about 21 parts oxygen in 100. Air out is about 16 parts oxygen and 4 parts carbon dioxide.
A bunch of grapes on a stalk is a good picture of alveoli on an airway.
A crushed sugar lump dissolves faster than a whole one, because more of its surface touches the water.
explanations.art: A lung drawn as an upside-down tree, with a zoomed circle showing a bunch of air bags wrapped in red capillaries, and blue and grey arrows crossing the thin wall.

explanations.concept: Blood: a liquid full of living cells
explanations.definition: Blood is a mix of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. It carries oxygen, food, waste, heat and messages round the body.
explanations.description: If you let a tube of blood settle, it separates into layers. A little more than half is plasma, a pale yellow liquid that is mostly water. Nearly all the rest is red blood cells. A thin layer in between holds white blood cells, which fight germs, and platelets, which plug cuts. A speck of blood the size of a pinhead holds about 5 million red blood cells. A red blood cell has no centre part, so there is more room inside for haemoglobin. Haemoglobin is a red protein with iron in it, and it is what grabs oxygen in the lungs and lets go of it where it is needed. Blood that is full of oxygen is bright red. Blood that has given up much of its oxygen is dark red, not blue. Red blood cells live for about four months. The red bone marrow inside your bones makes about 2 million new ones every second in an adult.
examples: Plasma carries food and carbon dioxide, and the red cells carry most of the oxygen.
Iron-rich food, such as ragi, dal, beetroot and green leaves, gives the body iron to build haemoglobin.
Your bone marrow is making new blood cells right now.
explanations.art: A tall test tube of settled blood showing a yellow plasma layer on top, a thin pale layer, and a thick red layer at the bottom, with labels.

explanations.concept: The heart's two sides: a double loop
explanations.definition: The heart is a muscle pump with four rooms. The right side sends blood to the lungs, and the left side sends blood to the rest of the body.
explanations.description: Your heart has two upper rooms called atria and two lower rooms called ventricles. The right side receives dark red blood that has given up its oxygen. It pumps this blood a short way to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen. The blood then comes back to the left side of the heart. The left side is the strong side, with a thicker wall, because it pushes blood all the way round the body, even to your toes. After the trip, the blood returns to the right side to start again. So the blood goes through the heart twice on one full round. Flaps called valves open and shut, and make the sound of a heartbeat, which is often written as lub-dub. One full round of the body takes about a minute at rest. The heart is about the size of your fist, and it sits in the middle of the chest, tilted a little to the left.
examples: Blood that is going to the lungs is low in oxygen. Blood that is coming back from the lungs is full of oxygen.
A fish has a heart with only two rooms and one loop. A bird has four rooms and two loops, like us.
The thick wall of the left side is why a heartbeat is felt most on the left of the chest.
explanations.art: A heart cut open showing four rooms, with blue arrows going to the lungs from the right side and red arrows going out to the body from the left side.

explanations.concept: Arteries, capillaries and veins: three kinds of road
explanations.definition: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, capillaries are thin vessels where cells receive oxygen, and veins carry blood back to the heart.
explanations.description: Arteries have thick, stretchy walls, because blood arrives in strong pushes. That is why you can feel a pulse in an artery. The arteries divide again and again into smaller and smaller tubes. The smallest are capillaries, so thin that red blood cells squeeze through in single file. A capillary wall is only one cell thick, so oxygen and food pass through into the cells around it, and carbon dioxide passes in. Almost every cell in your body is close to a capillary. Then the capillaries join up into veins. Veins have thinner walls, and small flaps inside that act like one-way doors, so blood cannot slip backwards when you are standing. When you walk, the muscles in your legs squeeze the veins and help to push blood up. The total length of all your blood vessels is often said to be about 100,000 kilometres, but that figure is an estimate.
examples: A paper cut that bleeds a little has opened a few capillaries.
The bluish lines on the back of your hand are veins just under the skin.
Standing still for a long time can make some people feel dizzy, because the blood pools in the legs.
explanations.art: A tree-like drawing of a vessel splitting from a thick artery into very thin capillaries and joining into a vein, with red cells in single file inside the capillary.

explanations.concept: How your body sets the pace: carbon dioxide is the signal
explanations.definition: Your breathing rate is set mostly by how much carbon dioxide is in your blood. Your heart rate follows nerve signals and chemical messengers.
explanations.description: You might think you breathe faster because you are running out of oxygen. In fact, the signal is mostly carbon dioxide. Busy muscles make more carbon dioxide, and it makes the blood slightly more acidic. Sensors in a part of the brain called the brainstem, and in large arteries in the neck, notice this change within seconds. They tell the breathing muscles to work harder. Your heart also gets the message. Nerve signals and a chemical messenger called adrenaline make the heart beat faster and push harder. So pulse and breathing rate rise together, because they answer the same call from the cells. When the cells quieten down, the carbon dioxide level falls, and both slow down again. This is why you cannot hold your breath for long. The urge to breathe grows as carbon dioxide builds up, long before oxygen runs low. Fit people have a lower resting pulse, because their heart pushes out more blood with each beat and does not need to beat as often.
examples: After a sprint, you keep panting for a while, because there is still extra carbon dioxide to clear.
A person who has run for years often has a resting pulse below 60 beats per minute.
Fear makes your heart race, because adrenaline reaches it even when you are not moving.
explanations.art: A runner with arrows from muscles to a small sensor in the neck and brain, then to a heart and lungs, each drawn with a speed dial turned up.

explanations.concept: Blood goes where it is needed: cold, warmth and posture
explanations.definition: The body sends more blood to the places that need it and less to the places that do not. It can narrow some blood vessels and widen others.
explanations.description: Tiny muscles in the walls of small arteries can squeeze them narrow or let them open wide. In the cold, the vessels near the skin narrow. Less blood reaches your fingers, so they turn pale and feel cold, and more blood stays near the heart and the other organs that must stay warm. In the heat, the vessels near the skin widen. More blood reaches the skin, your cheeks turn red, and heat escapes into the air. After a meal, more blood goes to the gut. During a run, more goes to the leg muscles. Gravity matters too. When you stand up, some blood sinks towards the legs, and the heart speeds up for a moment to keep enough blood going to the brain. This is why a pulse is a little higher standing than lying down. You can test how quickly blood returns to a fingertip. Press the nail until it turns white and let go. In a warm hand, the pink colour comes back in about one or two seconds.
examples: Pale, cold fingers on a winter morning in Shimla or Leh are the body protecting its middle.
Red cheeks after a game of kabaddi are widened vessels letting heat out.
A person who stands up too fast may see spots, because the blood has not caught up yet.
explanations.art: Two hands side by side, a warm pink one with wide vessels drawn beneath the skin, and a cold pale one with narrow vessels, and the heart in the middle with arrows.

explanations.concept: Thin air, thick blood: living high up
explanations.definition: Higher up a mountain, each breath has less oxygen. Over weeks, the body makes more red blood cells and adjusts its breathing to cope.
explanations.description: At sea level, air pressure is highest, and each breath is packed with oxygen. In Leh, at about 3,500 metres, the air pressure is only about two thirds as high, so each breath holds about two thirds as much oxygen. A visitor from Chennai or Madurai breathes faster, has a faster pulse and feels tired. After a few days, the kidneys release a messenger called erythropoietin, and the bone marrow makes more red blood cells. This takes weeks to finish, so mountaineers go up slowly. People whose families have lived in the Himalayas for thousands of years have changes in their genes that help them cope with thin air. Scientists found that one such gene change in Tibetans looks like one passed down from an extinct group of humans, the Denisovans. Some visitors get altitude sickness, with headache and sickness, and the cure is to rest or go lower. Anyone who feels very ill at height needs a doctor.
examples: Mountaineers spend days at a camp partway up before they go higher.
Some athletes train at high places to raise their red blood cell count.
People with anaemia feel breathless sooner, because they have fewer red blood cells to carry oxygen.
explanations.art: A mountain with three levels of air drawn as dots getting thinner higher up, and a small child at the bottom and top, with a breathing arrow bigger at the top.

explanations.concept: Other bodies, other ways of moving oxygen
explanations.definition: Different animals move oxygen in very different ways. Some have a heart and closed vessels like ours. Some have none.
explanations.description: An insect has no vessels that carry oxygen. Air goes directly into the body through tiny holes and small tubes, and the insect's blood only carries food and wastes. A fish has a heart with two rooms and sends blood in one loop through the gills. An octopus has three hearts and blood that is blue-green, because it carries oxygen with copper instead of iron. An earthworm has five pairs of muscular rings that squeeze blood along. A plant has no heart, but sap moves up from the roots and sugar moves down from the leaves. Whether any of these are better than ours is not a sensible question, because each fits the body that has it. A harder question is whether the number of heartbeats in a life is limited. Small animals such as mice beat their hearts about 600 times a minute and live a few years. Large animals such as elephants beat about 30 times a minute and live decades.
examples: A mouse heart beats about 600 times a minute, an elephant heart about 30.
A blue whale's heart can slow to only a few beats per minute during a deep dive.
A hummingbird's heart can beat well over 1,000 times a minute in flight.
explanations.art: A row of animals in a line, a mouse, a fish, an octopus, a person and an elephant, each with a small drawing of the heart or oxygen system and a number for beats per minute.

perspectives.explanation: In many mammals, the total number of heartbeats in a life is roughly similar, at around a billion, because small animals beat fast and live short lives. This suggests that something limits how many beats a heart can make.

Humans live far longer than the pattern predicts, with about 2 to 3 billion beats in a life, and many animals break the pattern. So the number of beats is probably a result of body size and energy use, not a fixed count.

agreed.text: Blood is pumped round the body in a closed loop, and goes through the heart twice on each full trip.
agreed.evidence: Harvey showed in 1628 that blood circulates. Malpighi saw capillaries in 1661. Modern scans show blood moving through the four heart rooms in order.

agreed.text: Every cell needs oxygen to release energy from food, and blood carries it there.
agreed.evidence: Lavoisier measured oxygen used up by breathing animals in the 1780s. Modern instruments measure oxygen in blood, and cells without oxygen soon stop working.

agreed.text: Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries most of the oxygen in blood.
agreed.evidence: Max Perutz worked out the shape of haemoglobin with X-rays around 1960 and saw where oxygen is held. Blood without red blood cells carries far less oxygen.

agreed.text: The air we breathe out has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than the air we breathe in.
agreed.evidence: Gas sensors measure about 21 parts oxygen in 100 in fresh air and about 16 in breathed-out air, with about 4 parts carbon dioxide.

agreed.text: Breathing rate is controlled mainly by the level of carbon dioxide in the blood.
agreed.evidence: People who breathe air with extra carbon dioxide breathe faster, while people who breathe air with less oxygen but normal carbon dioxide change much less at first.

agreed.text: The body sends more blood to the parts that are busy and less to the parts that are not.
agreed.evidence: Scans show blood flow rising in working muscles and in the gut after a meal, and falling in the skin of cold fingers.

challenging.claim: Blood in your veins is blue until it meets air.
challenging.who: Many people, and some school books.
challenging.for: Veins look blue under the skin, and diagrams colour them blue.
challenging.against: Blood is always some shade of red. Dark blood with less oxygen is dark red. Veins look blue because of how skin and light work together. Blood drawn from a vein in a needle is clearly dark red.

challenging.claim: We breathe out only carbon dioxide, and no oxygen.
challenging.for: Plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, so people often think we do the reverse, completely.
challenging.against: Breathed-out air is about 16 parts oxygen and 4 parts carbon dioxide in 100. That is why a person can give rescue breaths to another person.

challenging.claim: We breathe faster during exercise because we are running out of oxygen.
challenging.who: Many people, and some older books.
challenging.for: Oxygen is used faster during exercise, and tired people feel breathless.
challenging.against: The main signal is the carbon dioxide level in the blood, and the pH change it causes. Breathing rate rises before oxygen has fallen much.

challenging.claim: The pulse can tell a skilled reader about many diseases, as nadi pariksha says.
challenging.who: Practitioners of Ayurveda, and similar traditions in other countries.
challenging.for: Doctors in many traditions have read the pulse for thousands of years. Modern doctors read its rate, rhythm and strength, and find real clues in them.
challenging.against: Careful tests have not yet shown that pulse reading can tell the many kinds of illness that some traditions describe. Researchers continue to study it.

challenging.claim: The heart is where we think and feel, and the brain only helps.
challenging.who: Aristotle, and many cultures before and since.
challenging.for: A frightened or happy person feels the heart race or swell. The heart also has its own network of nerve cells.
challenging.against: Damage to the brain changes thinking, memory and feeling. A heart can be replaced by a transplant or a machine, and the person stays the same person.

big_questions.q: When you run, who decides to speed up your heart: you, your brain, or your muscles?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens when you try to slow your heart down on purpose, and what changes it when you are scared.

big_questions.q: The iron in your blood was made inside a star. Does that make a red blood cell part of the sky?
big_questions.hint: Think about where iron comes from, and how it got into the food you ate.

big_questions.q: Plants give out the oxygen that your blood carries. Whose oxygen is it?
big_questions.hint: Think about a leaf, the air in your lungs, and where the oxygen was an hour ago.

big_questions.q: Your heart started beating a few weeks after you began, long before you could think. Who or what was doing it?
big_questions.hint: Think about heart cells that beat on their own in a dish, and about what 'you' means.

big_questions.q: A mouse and an elephant have hearts with the same plan, but beat at very different speeds. What does that say about how a body is made?
big_questions.hint: Think about size, energy and how long it takes for blood to go round a small body or a big one.

big_questions.q: A visitor to Leh gasps on the stairs, while a child there runs. Who is stronger, and what does 'strong' mean?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air, the blood and how long each of them has lived there.

big_questions.q: Your pulse changes when you feel scared or excited. Does the body feel first, or does the mind?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have argued about this since the 1880s. Think about what you notice when you are startled.

big_questions.q: More than half of the women in India have anaemia. Why might it be so common, and who should fix it?
big_questions.hint: Think about food, who eats last in many homes, and what blood needs to be made.

story.title: Two Fingers on the Wrist
story.note: A made-up story. The children and the places in it are imagined, though Leh is a real town at about 3,500 metres. The science is real: thin air, a faster pulse, cold fingers and the nail test.
text: Arjun came to Leh from Madurai in the second week of May. The plane landed in a valley 3,500 metres above the sea. The sky was a darker blue than any sky he had ever seen. The second thing he noticed was his heart. It was knocking against his ribs as if he had run a race, and he had only walked to the car.

His cousin Dolma was ten, a year older than he was. She carried his bag up to the flat. There were twenty-two steps, and she did not even breathe hard. Arjun stopped at step twelve and held the railing, with his mouth open like a fish.
"Sit," said Dolma. "Your body does not know this air yet."
"What is wrong with the air? It looks the same."

"There is less in every breath," she said. She did not say less of what. She took his hand, and put two of his own fingers on the inside of his wrist. "Not the thumb. The thumb has a pulse of its own and it will fool you. Count for half a minute."

Arjun counted fifty-two. Dolma counted her own. She got forty. "Double them," she said. "A hundred and four for you, and eighty for me. Your heart is working harder than mine, and you are only sitting."

Dolma's grandmother, Ama-le, was drying apricots on a cloth by the window. She poured him salty butter tea and told him what to do. "Drink. Sleep. Go slowly for three days. Every breath up here carries a little less sky, and your body must learn how to find the rest." Then she took his hand and pressed her thumb on his fingernail until the pink went white. She let go and counted aloud. "One." The pink flooded back. "When the colour comes back fast, the blood is arriving. When it comes back slowly, the blood has gone somewhere else. Your fingers will tell you before your mouth does. And if hands ever go cold and white, never rub them. Warm them slowly, against your body."

Each morning for ten days, Arjun and Dolma sat on the roof and counted. The first morning it was a hundred and four. A week later it was ninety-two. By the third week it was eighty-eight, and he climbed all twenty-two steps and only laughed at the top.

In that third week, the channel stopped. The water that ran from the glacier to Ama-le's barley field came down a stone ditch, and something had blocked it high on the hill. The grown-ups were at the bazaar. The field would be dry by evening.
"I will go," said Dolma. "I know the path."

"I will come," said Arjun, and Dolma looked at him, and then she nodded. They climbed slowly. "Breathe in for two steps, out for two steps," she told him. He did it, and for the first time the hill did not beat him.

At the top, a slab of old ice and stones lay across the ditch. Dolma lay flat on the bank and pushed her arms into the stream up to the elbows. The water was so cold that it hurt, and then it stopped hurting. She heaved the slab aside. The water leapt past her, clear and loud, and ran down the hill towards the field.
She laughed, but the laugh was thin. "I am fine," she said. She dropped her woollen cap, and picked it up, and dropped it again.

Arjun looked at her hands. The tips of her fingers were the colour of candle wax. He took her first finger and pressed the nail until it turned white. He let go, and counted aloud as Ama-le had done. "One. Two. Three. Four." The nail stayed white.
"Ama-le said that slow means the blood has gone somewhere else," said Arjun. "It went to your middle, to keep your heart warm. Your body is saving the middle and letting go of the ends."
"I am not cold," said Dolma.
"Your fingers do not know that yet."

He did not rub her hands. Ama-le had said never to rub. He opened his jacket and tucked her hands under his arms, against his shirt, where it was warm. They sat on the bank in the loud sound of the water. Arjun felt her breaths slowing against his side. Slowly, the skin of her fingers lost its wax colour.
After a long time he tried the nail again. He pressed, and let go. "One," he said. The pink came back like a lamp being lit. "Two. There. It came."

They walked home slowly, breathing in for two steps and out for two. At the gate, Ama-le looked at Dolma's hands and then at Arjun. She said nothing. She pressed Dolma's nail, and nodded, and poured two cups of tea.

That night the water ran along the edge of the barley field, soaking the dry ground. Arjun lay in bed and put two fingers on his wrist. Eighty-eight. All through him, a red river that was never still was carrying the thin sky to the ends of him, and taking it back again. He had known the air for three weeks. He knew his cousin's hands because she had taught him how to find his own pulse first.
story.epiphany: When the body is cold, it sends blood away from the fingers to protect the middle. The slow return of colour in a pressed nail shows that the blood has gone elsewhere.
ask: Why did Arjun's pulse come down in the three weeks while he stayed in Leh?
What did the white fingernail tell Arjun that Dolma could not feel?
Why did Arjun warm Dolma's hands under his arms, and not by rubbing them?

experiments.title: The Pulse Detective: what changes your pulse and your breathing?
experiments.question: How do your pulse and your breathing change when you lie down, sit, stand and exercise, and how long do they take to settle afterwards?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In which situation will your pulse be highest? Will your breathing change as much as your pulse? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same child is tested every time, with the same two fingers on the same wrist. Every count lasts 15 seconds, and the pulse is counted first and the breaths second. The same stopwatch is used, at the same time of day, and the child has not just eaten a big meal. Only the situation changes, so any difference comes from the situation.
experiments.context: In this experiment you count your pulse and your breaths in eight situations: lying, sitting, standing, and five times after exercise. You find out what changes them, and how fast they come back to rest.

materials.item: a phone or kitchen clock with a stopwatch, to count 15 seconds
a mat or folded blanket to lie on
a low, sturdy step, such as the bottom stair or a firm stool about 20 centimetres high
a pencil and a notebook, with the results table drawn in it
a picture book for the child to look at while the parent counts breaths

experiments.safety: Use a low, firm step with no wobble, and keep a grown-up beside the child. Stop the step-ups at once if the child feels dizzy, has pain in the chest or cannot catch their breath. Any child with a heart or breathing condition should ask the doctor before doing the step-ups.
experiments.record: Fill the table as you go. Write the claim, the evidence and the reasoning at the end. Draw a line graph of the pulse per minute against the minutes after exercise.

setup.art: A child lying on a mat with a picture book, with a parent kneeling beside her holding a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Lie on a mat for two minutes. Then count your pulse for 15 seconds.

setup.art: The same child sitting, then standing, each with two fingers on her wrist and a parent holding the stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Do the same sitting for one minute, then standing for one minute.

setup.art: The child stepping up onto the bottom stair and back down, with a parent counting out loud.
setup.caption: 3. Step up and down for one minute, about one step-up every two seconds.

setup.art: The child sitting after exercise with two fingers on her wrist, and a notebook table with five rows beside her.
setup.caption: 4. Count your pulse and breaths straight away, and again each minute for four minutes.

flow.do: Show the child the results table. Ask for a guess and a reason for the pulse and for the breathing, before any counting. Write both down.
flow.say: We will count your pulse and your breaths in different situations. In which situation do you think your pulse will be highest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will count your pulse and your breaths. Where will your pulse be highest? Why do you think so?
flow.context: In this step you make a guess and give a reason, before any counting.

ask.q: Do you think your breathing will change as much as your pulse? Why?
good: Both will go up when I run, because I need more air.
Breathing will change more, because I can feel it.
The heart will change more, because it pumps blood everywhere.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write it down so the child can compare it with the result.

flow.do: Sit together. Show the child how to rest two fingers, not the thumb, on the inside of the wrist. Press gently until a small push is felt. Practise one 15-second count.
flow.say: Rest two fingers on the inside of your wrist. Do not use your thumb. Press gently until you feel a small push. I will say start and stop.
flow.kid: Two fingers on your wrist, not your thumb. Press gently. Feel the small push. Count when I say start.
flow.context: In this step you learn to find your pulse and count it for 15 seconds.
flow.parent: If the child cannot find it, slide the fingers a little towards the thumb side or press slightly harder. A heart is also easy to feel with a flat hand in the middle of the chest, a little to the left. With 2 to 4 children, work in pairs or threes: one is the subject, one counts the pulse, one holds the stopwatch and counts breaths, and everyone takes a turn at each job. Each child fills their own table, because pulses differ from child to child. One child with a parent: the child counts the pulse and the parent counts the breaths and keeps time.

check.q: Why do we use two fingers and not the thumb to find a pulse?
options: The thumb has a pulse of its own, which can fool you
The thumb is too big to press
Fingers are always warmer than thumbs
check.why: Your thumb has a small artery that beats, so you may count your own thumb's pulse by mistake. Two fingers pick up only the artery in your wrist. If you picked another answer, try again with a finger and a thumb on a friend's wrist, and compare.

flow.do: Ask the child to lie on the mat and look at the picture book for two minutes, quietly. Then say start, and the child counts the pulse for 15 seconds. Straight after, count the child's breaths by watching the belly rise for 15 seconds, without saying so. Write both numbers down.
flow.say: Lie on the mat and look at the book. Stay quiet for two minutes. Then count your pulse when I say start. Afterwards, I will tell you what else I counted.
flow.kid: Lie down and read the book. After two minutes, count your pulse for 15 seconds.
flow.context: In this step you count your pulse and your breaths while lying down.
flow.parent: Count breaths without telling the child during the count. People change how they breathe when they know it is being counted. Count one rise and fall as one breath. Tell the child afterwards, and talk about why we did it that way.
flow.think: Why might it be better that the child did not know you were counting their breaths?

flow.do: Ask the child to sit up on the mat for one minute without moving much. Then count the pulse for 15 seconds, and the breaths for 15 seconds. Write them down.
flow.say: Sit up and rest for one minute. Then we count again. Pulse first, and then breaths.
flow.kid: Sit up and rest for one minute. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.
flow.context: In this step you count your pulse and your breaths while sitting.

ask.q: Is your pulse the same as lying down? Why do you think that happened?
good: It is a bit higher, because I sat up.
It is the same, because I am still resting.

flow.do: Ask the child to stand still for one minute, with the arms by the sides and no leaning. Then count the pulse for 15 seconds, and the breaths for 15 seconds. Write them down.
flow.say: Stand up straight and still for one minute. Now count your pulse again, and then I count your breaths.
flow.kid: Stand still for one minute. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.
flow.context: In this step you count your pulse and your breaths while standing.
flow.parent: Most children find the standing pulse is a few beats higher, sometimes as much as 10 to 15. This is normal. If the child feels dizzy, sit down at once.

check.q: Standing gave a higher pulse than lying down. What is the best reason?
options: Blood sinks towards the legs, so the heart speeds up to keep it reaching the brain
Standing is hard exercise for the arms
The wrist is closer to the heart when standing
check.why: When you stand up, gravity pulls blood down into the legs. The heart beats a little faster so enough blood still reaches your head. If you picked another answer, think about which parts of your body are working harder when you stand still.

flow.do: Ask the child to step up onto the step and down again, about one step-up every two seconds, for one minute. A grown-up stays beside the child. At once, count the pulse for 15 seconds and the breaths for 15 seconds. Write them down.
flow.say: Step up and down for one minute. I will count with you. When I say stop, count your pulse straight away.
flow.kid: Step up and down for one minute. Stop. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.
flow.context: In this step you exercise for one minute, then count your pulse and breaths straight away.

ask.q: What do you notice in your chest and your breathing?
good: I am breathing fast and deep.

flow.parent: Count straight away, because the pulse starts to fall within seconds. A child may lose count when the pulse is fast. Count together for the first try. Stop at once if the child feels dizzy or has any pain. Do this in a cool, shaded room and not in the afternoon heat, because a hot room raises the pulse by itself. Typical rested school-child pulses are about 70 to 100 a minute and rise to about 110 to 150 after a minute of stepping, but yours may differ.

flow.do: Ask the child to sit quietly. At 1, 2, 3 and 4 minutes after stopping, count the pulse for 15 seconds and then the breaths for 15 seconds. Write each pair down.
flow.say: Sit still. We will count again at one minute, two minutes, three minutes and four minutes after you stopped. Look at how the numbers change.
flow.kid: Sit still. Count your pulse at 1, 2, 3 and 4 minutes.
flow.context: In this step you count your pulse and breaths each minute after exercise, to see how they come back to rest.
flow.parent: Use the stopwatch from the moment the step-ups stop. Most children are back close to their resting pulse by the fourth minute. A child who plays sport a lot often recovers a little faster. Start each 15-second count at the minute mark, so the pulse is counted from 1:00 to 1:15 and the breaths from 1:15 to 1:30. The pulse is a little lower in the second count of each pair, which is fine.

flow.do: Help the child turn each 15-second count into a count for one minute by multiplying by 4. Fill in the last two columns.
flow.say: Each count was for 15 seconds, and there are four of those in one minute. So multiply each number by 4. Write the answers in the table.
flow.kid: Multiply each count by 4. That gives you beats and breaths in one minute.
flow.context: In this step you change your counts into pulse and breaths per minute.
flow.parent: For a count of 22 beats in 15 seconds, 22 times 4 is 88. Breaths counted in 15 seconds are small numbers, so the answers are rough. That is fine. If two counts differ by only 1 beat, that is within the error of a 15-second count, so do not claim a change.

check.q: You counted 30 beats in 15 seconds after exercise. What is the pulse per minute?
check.why: There are four 15-second spells in one minute. 30 times 4 is 120. If you answered 45, you added 15 instead of multiplying.

flow.do: Ask the child to say or write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. Compare with the first guess. Do not give the explanation until the child has said what they think.
flow.say: What did you find? Which number was highest, and when? What do you think made the heart and the breathing go up together?
flow.kid: Tell me what you found. Which numbers went up? What do you think made them go up?
flow.context: In this step you write what you think, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What do your cells need more of when you run?

flow.parent: Good evidence points to numbers in the table. A good claim might be: my pulse and my breathing went up together, then came down together. The explanation of why comes after this, in the cards.
flow.think: If both go up together, what might be telling them to go up?

experiments.title: Cold Fingers: how fast does the pink come back?
experiments.question: How long does it take for the colour to return to a pressed fingernail when your hand is warm, at room temperature, or cold?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In which hand will the pink come back fastest? Which will be slowest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same finger (the middle finger) of the same hand is pressed every time, for the same two seconds, with the same pressure. The same person counts the seconds, starting the moment the finger is let go. Each hand temperature is tested three times, and the hand is left to settle between tests. Only the temperature of the hand changes.
experiments.context: In this experiment you press a fingernail until it goes white and time how fast the pink returns. You test a warm hand, a room-temperature hand and a cold hand. It shows where your blood goes when you are cold.

materials.item: a bowl of warm tap water, comfortable for the hand and not hot (in summer, tap water may already be warm: use it as it is)
a bowl of cold tap water with 5 or 6 ice cubes in it (ice trays from the fridge are enough)
a clean towel
a phone or kitchen clock with a stopwatch, or a helper who counts 'one and, two and' out loud
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Keep the hand in the cold water for one minute only, and never more than two minutes. A grown-up watches the clock. Stop at once if the hand hurts or goes very white or numb. Do not do the cold part with a child who has poor circulation, and ask the doctor first if you are not sure. Never rub a very cold hand hard. Warm it gently.
experiments.record: Write the three times for each hand and the colour of the fingertips. Then write which hand was fastest, which was slowest, and why you think so. Say which room you did it in and whether the weather was hot, cool or damp.

setup.art: A child's hand resting in a bowl of warm water, with a clock beside the bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Rest one hand in warm water for two minutes. Dry it with a towel.

setup.art: A parent pressing a child's fingernail until it turns white, with the pink colour beside it on other fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Press a fingernail for two seconds until it goes white. Let go.

setup.art: A parent holding a stopwatch while the child's pressed fingernail turns pink again.
setup.caption: 3. Count the seconds until the nail is as pink as the finger beside it.

setup.art: A child's hand in a bowl of cold water with ice cubes, with a parent watching a clock.
setup.caption: 4. Put the same hand in cold water for one minute. Dry it. Test the nail again.

flow.do: Show the child how a pressed nail goes white. Ask for a guess and a reason for the warm hand, the room-temperature hand and the cold hand. Write them down.
flow.say: We will press a fingernail and time how fast the pink comes back. In which hand do you think it will come back fastest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will press a nail and time the pink coming back. Which hand will be fastest? Why?
flow.context: In this step you guess before you test.

ask.q: What do you think happens to the blood in your fingers when they are cold?

flow.parent: Accept any guess with a reason. A common idea is that blood freezes or stops. Do not correct it. Let the test show. With 2 to 4 children, work in pairs: one child is the hand, one presses and times. Share the two bowls, but run two pairs at the same time only if you have a helper to watch each cold-water minute. Every child tests their own hand, because skin and nails differ.

flow.do: Ask the child to rest the left hand in warm water for two minutes, then dry it. Press the nail of the middle finger firmly for two seconds, until it goes white. Let go and count the seconds until the nail looks as pink as the finger beside it. Do this three times. Use the left hand and the same finger for every test.
flow.say: Rest your hand in warm water for two minutes. Dry it. I will press your nail for two seconds and let go. Watch the pink come back, and I will count.
flow.kid: Put your hand in warm water for two minutes. Dry it. Ask a grown-up to press and time your nail.
flow.context: In this step you time the pink returning in a warm hand.
flow.parent: Count in half seconds if you can, saying one, and, two, and. Start counting the moment the finger is released. A warm hand often takes only about one second. Use the same finger, the same press and the same counter each time. Normal pink usually returns in about 1 to 2 seconds, so the differences are small and you must count carefully. A helper can say 'pink!' when the colour is back while the timer runs. If the nail colour is hard to see, press the soft pad of the fingertip instead and watch it go from pale to pink, and always use the same spot.

flow.do: Ask the child to rest the same left hand on the table for three minutes. This lets it settle back to normal. Press the same finger for two seconds and time the pink three times. Write the times down.
flow.say: Now rest the same hand on the table for three minutes. We press and time the nail in the same way.
flow.kid: Rest the same hand on the table for three minutes. Press and time the nail again.
flow.context: In this step you time the pink returning in a hand at room temperature.
flow.parent: A hand at room temperature is usually between the warm and the cold results. If the room is very cold or very hot, the result may be different. Write the room down in your notes.

flow.do: A grown-up watches the clock. The child puts the same hand into the iced water for one minute. Take it out, dry it, and at once press the nail for two seconds and time the pink three times. Look at the colour of the fingertips.
flow.say: Put your hand in the cold water for one minute. I will watch the clock. Take it out and dry it. Then we press and time the nail.
flow.kid: Put your hand in cold water for one minute. Dry it. Then press and time the nail.
flow.context: In this step you time the pink returning in a cold hand.

ask.q: What do you notice about the colour and the feel of your fingertips?
good: The pink took longer to come back.

flow.parent: Do the three presses quickly, because the hand starts to warm up at once. If the times are all similar, note the colour of the fingertips as well. Pale, waxy fingertips are a clear sign. Stop the test if the hand hurts. A cold hand should be slower, but the size of the change differs from child to child, typically from about 2 seconds to 4 seconds or more. If it does not change at all, the water was not cold enough, or the hand warmed up while you dried it. Write that down honestly and try again with more ice.

flow.do: Gently warm the cold hand under the other arm for two minutes. Press the nail again. Write down how long the pink takes now, and what the fingertips look like.
flow.say: Tuck your cold hand under your other arm, against your side. Wait two minutes. Then we press and time the nail once more.
flow.kid: Warm your cold hand under your arm. Then test the nail again.
flow.context: In this step you warm the hand up and see the blood return.
flow.parent: Do not rub the hand hard. Warm it gently. The pink should return faster as the hand warms, and the fingertips should look pinker. This is a good place to talk about how cold fingers feel painful as they warm.

flow.do: Ask the child to write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. Compare with the first guess. Do not explain until the child has said what they think.
flow.say: What did you find? Which hand was fastest? Where do you think the blood went when your hand was cold?
flow.kid: Tell me what you found. Which hand was fastest? Where do you think the blood went?
flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: The pink came back slowly in the cold hand. What does this show?
options: Less blood reached the fingertips while the hand was cold
The nail had frozen
The finger had stopped working for ever
check.why: A pressed nail turns white because the blood is squeezed out of the tiny vessels under it. The pink returns when new blood arrives. Slow return means that blood arrives slowly. In the cold, the small vessels near the skin narrow. If you picked another answer, notice that the colour came back as the hand warmed.

experiments.title: Big Surface, Fast Swap: why are lungs so wide?
experiments.question: Does the same amount of sugar dissolve faster as one lump, as crushed bits, or as a powder?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which glass will clear first, the lump, the crushed bits or the powder? Which will be last? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each glass holds 100 millilitres of the same warm tap water. Each glass gets one sugar lump's worth of the same sugar. No one stirs any glass. The glasses are started at the same moment and checked at the same times. Only the size of the pieces changes, so any difference comes from the size.
results_table: Time until all the sugar has gone (minutes)
experiments.context: In this experiment you dissolve the same amount of sugar as a lump, as crushed bits and as a powder. It shows why the lungs are built from hundreds of millions of tiny air bags and not from one big bag.

materials.item: 3 clear glasses, the same size
3 plain white sugar cubes, the same size (or 3 equal pieces of rock sugar (mishri), which dissolve more slowly)
warm tap water, comfortable to touch, about 300 millilitres in all (mix hot and cold water from a jug until it is comfortable)
a measuring cup or a small jug
a clean cloth and a rolling pin or a heavy spoon for crushing, and a clean mortar or a mixer jar for the powder
a phone stopwatch

experiments.safety: Use warm water that is not hot. A grown-up grinds the powder in a clean mortar or a mixer jar, because the blades are sharp. Do not drink the sugar water if the glasses were not food-clean, and keep the sugar away from ants.
experiments.record: Write the time for each glass. Draw each glass at the end. Say how the size of the pieces changed the time. Say how long a glass had to be clear and what you saw at the bottom.

setup.art: Three glasses in a row labelled A, B and C, each with 100 millilitres of water.
setup.caption: 1. Pour 100 millilitres of warm water into each of three glasses.

setup.art: Three small piles of sugar on a tray: a whole lump, a pile of crushed bits and a pile of fine powder.
setup.caption: 2. Keep one lump whole. Crush one into bits. Grind one into powder.

setup.art: A child dropping the three sugars into the three glasses at the same moment, with a stopwatch beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Add all three at the same moment. Start the stopwatch. Do not stir.

setup.art: The three glasses after several minutes: the powder glass clear, the crushed glass nearly clear, the lump glass still with sugar at the bottom.
setup.caption: 4. Look every minute. Write down when each glass is clear.

flow.do: Show the three kinds of sugar. Ask the child for a guess and a reason about which will clear first, and which last. Write them down.
flow.say: We have the same amount of sugar in three forms. Which glass do you think will clear first? Which will be last? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Same sugar, three forms. Which glass clears first? Which last? Why?
flow.context: In this step you guess, with a reason, before you test.

ask.q: What is different between the three sugars?
good: One is powder, so it has many small pieces.

flow.parent: Accept any guess with a reason. Some children think that more pieces will take longer, because there is more to dissolve. The test will show. With 2 to 4 children: each child drops one sugar into one glass (A, B or C), and a fourth child, or the parent, runs the stopwatch and writes the times. Swap jobs and repeat if there is time. One child with a parent: the child drops all three and the parent keeps time.

flow.do: Pour 100 millilitres of warm water into each glass. Mark the glasses A, B and C. Ask the child to wrap one cube in the cloth and crush it into bits. Keep every bit. A grown-up grinds one cube into a fine powder.
flow.say: Pour the same amount of warm water into each glass. Glass A gets a whole lump. Glass B gets a crushed lump. Glass C gets a powdered lump.
flow.kid: Pour water into three glasses. A is the lump. B is crushed. C is powder.
flow.context: In this step you set up the three glasses and prepare the three sugars.
flow.parent: The water in each glass must be at the same warmth. Pour from one jug to be sure. Do not use hot water, because hot water makes everything dissolve fast and the difference is hard to see. Each glass gets the sugar of one whole cube (about one level teaspoon). Do not lose any bits or powder, because less sugar would clear faster and spoil the test.

check.q: Why do we use the same amount of sugar in each glass?
options: So that only the size of the pieces is different
So that the sugar tastes the same
So that the glasses look the same
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here the size of the pieces changes, so the amount of sugar must stay the same. If you picked another answer, remember that a fair test is about finding the reason for a difference.

flow.do: Drop the three sugars into the glasses at the same moment and start the stopwatch. Do not stir. Tip in the powder gently so it does not splash.
flow.say: Ready? Drop them in together, on three. One, two, three. Start the stopwatch. Do not stir, because stirring would hide the difference.
flow.kid: Drop all three in together. Start the stopwatch. Do not stir.
flow.context: In this step you start all three glasses at once.
flow.parent: Stirring spreads the sugar and hides the effect of the size of the pieces, so keep the spoons away.

flow.do: Every minute, look at the glasses and write down which sugar is gone and which is not. Note the time when each glass is completely clear. Stop at 15 minutes.
flow.say: Look at the glasses every minute. Which one has cleared? Which one still has sugar? Write the time when each one is clear.
flow.kid: Look every minute. Write down the time when each glass is clear.
flow.context: In this step you watch the sugar dissolve and write down the times.

ask.q: What do you notice about the water around each lump?
good: The water near the lump looks wavy.
There are fewer bits in glass C.

flow.parent: Call a glass 'clear' when you cannot see any grains at the bottom when you tilt it. The powder may be clear in about a minute, and may sit in a clump at first. The crushed bits take a few minutes. A plain sugar cube in warm water typically takes about 3 to 10 minutes without stirring, and mishri takes longer. If the lump is not gone after 15 minutes, write 'more than 15'. That is a good result. If all three finish at about the same time, the water was probably too hot: try again with cooler water.

flow.do: Ask the child to write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. Then ask how this could link to lungs. Do not explain until the child has said what they think.
flow.say: What did you find? Which glass cleared first? Think about how much of the sugar touches the water in each glass. What do you think made the difference?
flow.kid: Tell me what you found. Which glass cleared first? Why do you think so?
flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw and why.

check.q: The powder dissolved fastest. What is the best reason?
options: More of the sugar touches the water at once
Powder is lighter than a lump
Powder is sweeter than a lump
check.why: Sugar dissolves only where it touches water. Breaking it into tiny pieces makes much more of its surface touch the water, so it dissolves faster. Lungs use the same idea, with a huge surface for oxygen to cross. If you picked another answer, think about which part of the sugar can meet the water in a lump.

activities.title: Pulse Points: where else can you feel your heartbeat?

materials.item: a clean, dry hand, a partner if possible, and a phone or kitchen clock with a stopwatch

activities.safety: On the neck, use one finger very lightly on one side only. Never press hard on the neck, and never press both sides at once.

schedule.what: Find the pulse at the wrist, the temple, the side of the neck and the chest. Compare the four, then compare them again after 20 star jumps.

activities.record: Write which places you found a pulse, and which place was the easiest. Write the number of beats in 15 seconds at two places, at rest and after 20 star jumps, and compare.
activities.context: In this activity you hunt for your pulse in four places on your body. It shows that the same heartbeat reaches all of them.

setup.art: A child with two fingers on the inside of her wrist and a speech bubble that says here.
setup.caption: 1. Find the pulse on the inside of the wrist.

setup.art: The same child touching the side of her forehead near the eye, in front of her ear.
setup.caption: 2. Find the pulse at the temple, in front of the ear.

setup.art: The same child with one finger lightly on the side of her neck, and a note that says very light, one side only.
setup.caption: 3. Find the pulse at the side of the neck with one very light finger.

flow.do: Ask the child to guess, with a reason, whether the pulse will be the same at every place. Then find the pulse at the wrist, then at the temple, just in front of the ear. Next, very lightly at the side of the neck. Last, with a flat hand on the chest. Count for 15 seconds at the wrist and at the neck. A partner can count one place each, at the same moment. Compare the numbers. Then do 20 star jumps and count again at the same two places.
flow.say: Find your pulse at your wrist. Now try in front of your ear, at your temple. Try very lightly on one side of your neck. Last, put a flat hand on your chest. Which is easiest?
flow.kid: Find your pulse at four places. Which one is easiest? Count at two places and compare.
flow.context: In this step you find your pulse in four places and compare them.

ask.q: Why might the same number of beats show up in all four places?

flow.parent: The numbers at the different places should match, within one or two beats. The pulse is a pressure wave from one heartbeat, so it arrives everywhere almost at once. On the neck, use a single light finger and only on one side. With 2 to 4 children, work in pairs: one counts the wrist and the other the neck of the same person at the same moment, then swap. After exercise the numbers are higher, but both places should still match within one or two beats, and the pulse is easier to find.

check.q: You count 21 beats in 15 seconds at your wrist and 22 at your temple. What does this suggest?
options: It is the same heart beating, so the counts should be close
Your temple has its own heart
One of the counts must be wrong by a lot
check.why: A pulse is a wave of pressure from one heart, so it reaches your wrist and temple together. A difference of one or two is just a counting slip. If you picked another answer, count again at both places.

activities.title: Who Breathes Fastest? A breath count of the family

materials.item: a phone or kitchen clock with a stopwatch
a notebook and a pencil
a resting pet, a baby or a younger brother or sister, a grown-up and a grandparent, if you can ask them

activities.safety: Count only resting or sleeping people and pets, and watch from a little way off. Do not wake a sleeping baby or an animal, and do not touch an unfamiliar animal. Wash your hands after touching any pet. If a child is allergic to fur, count that pet from a distance.

schedule.what: Count the breaths of at least four resting beings for 15 seconds each. Multiply by 4. Draw a bar chart.

activities.record: Write each name, the count for 15 seconds, and the breaths per minute. Draw a bar chart of breaths per minute for each being.
activities.context: In this activity you count the breaths of different resting beings in your home and make a bar chart. It shows that breathing rate depends on the size and age of the body.

setup.art: A child watching a sleeping cat's side rise and fall, with a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Watch a resting being's chest or belly rise and fall for 15 seconds.

setup.art: A notebook table with four names and numbers, and a hand pointing to the multiply by 4 column.
setup.caption: 2. Write the count. Multiply by 4 to get breaths per minute.

setup.art: A bar chart with one bar for each being, in different colours.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar for each being on a bar chart.

flow.do: Ask the child to guess who breathes fastest and who breathes slowest, from a list of the beings to be counted. Write the guesses down with the reasons.
flow.say: Who do you think breathes fastest in our home? Who breathes slowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Who breathes fastest in our home? Who slowest? Why?
flow.context: In this step you guess who breathes fastest before counting.
flow.parent: Children often guess the biggest being breathes fastest, or the loudest. Let them guess. Do not correct.

flow.do: Ask the child to watch each resting being for 15 seconds and count the rises of the chest or belly. Write each count down and multiply by 4. Draw a bar for each in a bar chart.
flow.say: Watch a resting person or pet for 15 seconds. Count each time the chest or belly rises. Multiply your number by 4. Then draw a bar.
flow.kid: Watch for 15 seconds. Count each rise. Multiply by 4. Draw a bar.
flow.context: In this step you count the breaths of several resting beings and draw a bar chart.

ask.q: What pattern do you notice between age or size and breathing rate?

flow.parent: Usual resting rates are about 30 to 40 breaths a minute for a young baby, about 18 to 25 for a school child, about 12 to 20 for an adult, and about 15 to 30 for a resting dog or cat. Animals that have just played will be faster, so count only those who are calm. Breath counts over 15 seconds are rough: a miss of one breath changes the answer by 4. For steadier numbers count for 30 seconds and multiply by 2. With 2 to 4 children, each child counts different beings, or two children count the same being and compare their numbers. With one child, the parent keeps time.

check.q: Which being would you expect to breathe fastest while resting?
options: A young baby
A grandparent
A grown-up
check.why: Smaller bodies and younger bodies usually breathe faster at rest. A young baby breathes about twice as fast as a grown-up. If you picked another answer, check your counts against the bar chart.

activities.title: Iron for the Blood: catch the iron in a bowl of cereal

materials.item: a cup of breakfast cereal that lists iron on its nutrition label, such as a fortified corn flake, and a cup of plain puffed rice (murmura) with no added iron, for comparison
a strong magnet, such as a neodymium magnet or one from an old loudspeaker, and a strong plastic zip bag to hold it
two clear bowls and warm water
a white plate or sheet of paper

activities.safety: A grown-up handles any strong magnet, and keeps it away from phones, watches, cards and anyone with a pacemaker. Strong magnets can pinch fingers and snap together hard. Small strong magnets must never be swallowed. Do not eat the cereal soup afterwards.

schedule.what: Crush cereal in warm water, stir with a magnet in a bag for 10 minutes, then look for tiny dark flecks. Repeat with plain puffed rice to compare.

activities.record: Draw the magnet bag at the end of each test. Write whether you found flecks in the cereal and in the puffed rice, how many, and what the nutrition label said about iron.
activities.context: In this activity you try to pull the iron out of a breakfast cereal with a magnet. Iron is one of the things blood needs to make haemoglobin.

setup.art: A bowl of crushed cereal in warm water, with a spoon.
setup.caption: 1. Crush a cup of cereal in warm water until it is a soft soup.

setup.art: A strong magnet inside a zip bag, being slowly swirled through the soup.
setup.caption: 2. Stir slowly with the magnet in the bag for 10 minutes.

setup.art: The zip bag held over a white plate, with tiny dark flecks stuck to its outside.
setup.caption: 3. Lift out the bag and look at tiny dark flecks stuck to it.

flow.do: Show the child the nutrition label and find the line for iron. Ask the child to guess whether a magnet can pull iron out of a soft, wet cereal, and why.
flow.say: This cereal has iron added to it, as a label says. Do you think a magnet can pull iron out of a soft, wet cereal? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The label says this cereal has iron. Can a magnet pull it out? Why?
flow.context: In this step you read the label and guess before you try.
flow.parent: Iron added to cereal is often a fine iron powder, which is magnetic. Not every cereal and not every magnet will show it. The magnet must be strong. If nothing shows up, that is a real result. This works best with a cereal whose label shows a good share of the daily iron, and with a strong magnet. A fridge magnet will not do. If you cannot find a strong magnet, borrow one from a hardware shop or an old speaker, or skip this activity and read the nutrition label alone.

flow.do: A grown-up helps the child to crush the cereal to a fine powder. Mix it with warm water in one bowl, to make a thin soup. Put the magnet in the zip bag and seal it. Stir the soup slowly with the bag for 10 minutes. With 2 to 4 children, take turns stirring for 2 or 3 minutes each.
flow.say: Crush the cereal into the warm water until it is soft. Seal the magnet in the bag. Stir slowly with the bag for 10 minutes.
flow.kid: Crush the cereal in warm water. Stir with the magnet in a bag for 10 minutes.
flow.context: In this step you stir the cereal soup with a magnet in a bag.
flow.parent: Stir slowly, so the iron has time to stick. Stay away from phones, watches and cards with the magnet.

flow.do: Lift the bag out of the soup. Hold it over a white plate and look at its outside for tiny dark flecks. Wipe them off onto the plate to see them better. Wash and dry the bag.
flow.say: Lift out the bag and look at its outside. Do you see tiny dark flecks? Those could be iron. Wipe them onto the white plate.
flow.kid: Lift out the bag. Look for tiny dark flecks on the outside.
flow.context: In this step you look for the iron that the magnet caught.

ask.q: Why do you think your body needs iron?

flow.parent: If you see flecks, they are likely to be iron powder. If you see none, the magnet may be too weak or the cereal may not hold much loose iron. The iron in your blood is not a magnet. It is held inside haemoglobin.

check.q: The magnet caught tiny dark flecks. Why does the body need iron?
options: Iron is a part of haemoglobin, which carries oxygen
Iron makes bones bend
Iron makes blood watery
check.why: Each haemoglobin molecule has iron at its heart. This is where oxygen grabs on. Without enough iron, the body makes less haemoglobin, so less oxygen can be carried. If you picked another answer, look at the haemoglobin card.

flow.do: Crush the plain puffed rice in warm water in the second bowl. Stir it with the clean bag and magnet for 5 minutes. Look for flecks in the same way. Compare the two plates.
flow.say: Now we do the same with puffed rice that has no added iron. Will the magnet catch flecks this time?
flow.kid: Do the same with plain puffed rice. Do you find flecks again? Compare the two plates.
flow.context: In this step you test a food with no added iron, so you can compare.

ask.q: Why do you think your body needs iron?

flow.parent: If a second magnet is at hand, two children can stir both bowls at the same time. The puffed rice should show no flecks, or far fewer, which is what makes the cereal result believable. If neither shows flecks, say so: the magnet may be too weak.

check.q: The magnet caught tiny dark flecks. Why does the body need iron?
options: Iron is a part of haemoglobin, which carries oxygen
Iron makes bones bend
Iron makes blood watery
check.why: Each haemoglobin molecule has iron at its heart. This is where oxygen grabs on. Without enough iron, the body makes less haemoglobin, so less oxygen can be carried. If you picked another answer, look at the haemoglobin card.

activities.title: Hand Up, Hand Down: where does the blood pool?

materials.item: your two hands, a clock and a pencil

schedule.what: Hold one hand high and one hand low for one minute and compare the colour and the veins. Swap hands and repeat, then time how fast the veins fill.

activities.record: Draw the back of each hand after one minute, both times. Write the colour and whether the veins stood out, and how many seconds the veins took to fill after you lowered the raised hand.
activities.context: In this activity you hold one hand high and one hand low, and see what gravity does to your blood. It shows how veins and valves lift blood up your body.

setup.art: A child with one arm raised above her head and the other hanging down by her side.
setup.caption: 1. Hold one hand high and one hand low for one minute.

setup.art: The child bringing both hands in front of her face and comparing the backs of them.
setup.caption: 2. Bring both hands in front of you. Compare the colour and the veins.

flow.do: Ask the child to guess how the two hands will look after one minute, and why. Then hold one hand high above the head and the other hanging down by the side for one minute. Bring both in front of the face and compare the colour and the veins on the backs. Then lower the raised hand and count the seconds until its veins fill. Rest for two minutes, swap the hands (the other hand up this time), and repeat, to check that it is the position that matters and not the hand.
flow.say: Do you think the two hands will look the same after one minute? Why do you think so? Hold one hand up high and one down low. After one minute, look at both.
flow.kid: Guess how the hands will look. Hold one hand up and one down for one minute. Then compare them.
flow.context: In this activity you hold one hand up and one down, then compare them.

ask.q: What do you notice about the veins and the colour?
good: The low hand is pinker and the veins stand out.

flow.parent: Usually the hanging hand looks pinker, with veins that stand out, and the raised hand looks paler, with flatter veins. Gravity pulls blood down. The effect is easy to see if you lower the raised hand afterwards and watch the veins fill. If the veins are hard to see on darker skin, compare the colour of the palms and fingertips, how full or puffy the fingers look, or how tight a ring or bangle feels. The veins typically fill in about 5 to 15 seconds. With 2 to 4 children, work in pairs so that one child compares and the other times.

check.q: The low hand looked pinker, with veins that stood out. Why?
options: Gravity pulled more blood down into that hand
The low hand worked harder
The low hand had the heart nearer
check.why: Blood weighs something, so gravity pulls it down. In the raised hand it drains towards the heart. In the hanging hand, veins fill. If you picked another answer, think about which hand was further from the heart.

activities.title: Breathe Through a Straw: what narrow airways feel like

materials.item: a clean plastic or paper drinking straw
a stopwatch on a phone or a clock
a chair

activities.safety: A grown-up stays with the child the whole time. Stop at once if the child feels dizzy, panicky or short of breath, and take the straw away. Skip this activity for any child with asthma or a breathing problem. Use a clean straw for each child, and use it only once. Marching is optional: a child who feels any discomfort should only sit and breathe through the straw.

schedule.what: Count pulse and breaths sitting. Breathe through a straw for one minute, then march on the spot for 20 seconds. Rest, and march for 20 seconds without the straw to compare.

activities.record: Write the pulse and the breaths in 15 seconds before and after, with and without the straw, and how each felt. Write one sentence on what you learned about people whose airways are narrow.
activities.context: In this activity you breathe through a straw to feel what narrow airways are like. In a person with asthma, the airways tighten. It shows why breathing hard work needs more effort.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with a straw between her lips and a hand pinching her nose, with a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Sit and breathe in and out through a straw for one minute.

setup.art: The same child marching on the spot, still breathing through the straw, with the grown-up watching.
setup.caption: 2. March on the spot for 20 seconds. Then stop and take the straw away.

flow.do: Count the child's resting pulse for 15 seconds and write it down. Ask for a guess and a reason about how breathing through a straw will feel, and how it will change the pulse.
flow.say: First, count your pulse sitting. Now guess. How will it feel to breathe through a straw? Will your pulse change? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count your pulse. How will breathing through a straw feel? Why?
flow.context: In this step you count a resting pulse and guess.
flow.parent: Take the pulse before the straw. Tell the child they can stop at any time by taking out the straw. Each child counts their own pulse and a partner counts the breaths over 15 seconds.

flow.do: With a grown-up beside, the child breathes through the straw for one minute, with the nose gently pinched. Then the child marches on the spot for 20 seconds, still using the straw. Stop and take the straw out. Count the pulse for 15 seconds.
flow.say: Pinch your nose gently and breathe through the straw for one minute. Then march on the spot for 20 seconds. If you feel dizzy, stop at once.
flow.kid: Breathe through the straw for one minute. March for 20 seconds. Stop if you feel dizzy.
flow.context: In this step you breathe through a straw and then march.

ask.q: What was it like to breathe through such a narrow tube?
good: I felt like I could not get enough air.

flow.parent: Most children find the straw hard even sitting. Remember that some children and adults live with narrower airways every day. An inhaler widens the airways quickly. This is a good moment to talk about being kind to someone who is short of breath.

check.q: Why did the straw make breathing hard work?
options: The air has to squeeze through a very narrow tube
The straw takes oxygen out of the air
