The straw makes the lungs smaller
check.why: The air still has oxygen, but a narrow tube slows the air down, so the breathing muscles must work harder. In asthma, the airways tighten in the same way. If you picked another answer, remember that the straw only changes the width.

flow.do: Rest until the pulse is back to the first resting number, about 3 to 5 minutes. Then the child marches on the spot for 20 seconds with no straw, breathing normally. Count the pulse for 15 seconds and the breaths for 15 seconds, and compare how it felt with the straw march.
flow.say: Rest until you feel normal. Now we march for the same 20 seconds, with no straw. How is it different?
flow.kid: Rest, then march for 20 seconds with no straw. Count your pulse. How did it feel different?
flow.context: In this step you do the same marching without the straw, so you can compare.
flow.parent: Do the marching without the straw second, so the comparison is fair, and keep the marching time the same. With 2 to 4 children, only one child breathes through a straw at a time while the others watch, count and time, and each child has their own clean straw. The pulse numbers may be similar, because 20 seconds is short, but the effort and the breathing usually feel very different. Say so, and explain that pulse counts are rough.

check.q: Why did the straw make breathing hard work?
options: The air has to squeeze through a very narrow tube
The straw takes oxygen out of the air
The straw makes the lungs smaller
check.why: The air still has oxygen, but a narrow tube slows the air down, so the breathing muscles must work harder. In asthma, the airways tighten in the same way. If you picked another answer, remember that the straw only changes the width.

activities.title: A Calm Story and a Scary Story: does feeling change the pulse?

materials.item: a stopwatch on a phone or a clock
two short stories, one calm and one exciting with a lot of suspense, each about two minutes to read out loud (a bedtime story and an adventure chase will do)

schedule.what: Count the resting pulse three times to see how much it varies. Then count the pulse during a calm story and during a suspenseful story, with a helper holding the wrist. Compare.

activities.record: Write the three resting counts, then the pulse for each story. Write whether it changed by more than the resting counts varied, and how sure you are, given that pulse counts are rough.
activities.context: In this activity you listen to a calm story and an exciting story, and count the pulse during each. It tests whether feelings, and not only movement, change your pulse.

setup.art: A child sitting on a mat with two fingers on her wrist, listening to a parent reading a book.
setup.caption: 1. Listen to a calm story. Count your pulse in the last 15 seconds.

setup.art: The same child sitting on the edge of the mat with wide eyes, listening to a parent read a spooky part.
setup.caption: 2. Listen to an exciting story. Count your pulse in the last 15 seconds.

flow.do: Ask the child to sit still and rest. Count the resting pulse for 15 seconds three times, one minute apart, to see how much it varies on its own. Read a calm story for two minutes, and then count the pulse for 15 seconds. Rest for two minutes. Read a suspenseful story for two minutes, and count the pulse again in the last 15 seconds. A helper holds the child's wrist and counts, so that the child can just listen.
flow.say: Do you think a scary story could change your pulse even if you sit still? Why do you think so? Listen to the calm story first. Count your pulse in the last 15 seconds.
flow.kid: Listen to a calm story. Count your pulse. Then listen to an exciting story. Count again.
flow.context: In this activity you test whether an exciting story changes your pulse.

ask.q: What do you think is telling your heart to speed up?

flow.parent: The change may be small, only a few beats, and a count over 15 seconds can be wrong by about four. Say so honestly. If the numbers are about the same, that is also a result. Strong feelings such as fear release adrenaline, which can raise the pulse even when the body is still. The three resting counts show the 'noise': if they differ by 2 or 3 beats on their own, a story change of that size means nothing. With 2 to 4 children, work in pairs: one listens, one counts, then swap; all can listen to the same story. One child with a parent: the parent reads and then counts, so read the story in advance and count in the last 15 seconds of reading, or use a recorded story. Use the same position and time for both stories.

check.q: The pulse was a little higher in the exciting story. What is a fair thing to say?
options: The change might be real, but the count is rough, so we should test more times
The story proved that feelings change the pulse
The pulse never changes when you sit
check.why: A 15-second count is rough, so a small difference could be chance. A fair scientist repeats the test. If you picked another answer, remember to be careful about what one test can show.

activities.safety: Choose a story that is exciting but not frightening, with no horror, and stop at once if the child becomes upset or scared. Tell the child it is only a story and that it is fine to say stop.

games.title: Faster, Same or Slower? A card game about pulse and breathing
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card shows a situation. You decide whether the pulse and breathing go faster, stay about the same or go slower, and a reason on the back tells you why.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, with three tokens in front of each player: faster, about the same, slower.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud, while the others each put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone puts a token face down.

setup.art: The players turning their tokens over together, and the reader turning the card to read the back.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. Read the back. Score a point if you were right.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a situation on the front, and the verdict and the reason on the back

items.f: You are sound asleep in bed at night. What happens to your pulse and breathing, compared with sitting awake?
items.b: Slower. Your cells need less energy while you sleep, so the heart and lungs slow down below the usual resting rate.

items.f: You are sitting and reading a story book. What happens, compared with your resting rate?
items.b: About the same. Sitting and reading is what we call resting, so this is your usual resting rate.

items.f: You stand up quickly after lying on the floor. What happens to your pulse for a moment?
items.b: Faster. Gravity pulls blood down to the legs, so the heart beats faster for a few beats to keep blood reaching the brain.

items.f: You run to catch a bus. What happens to your pulse and breathing?
items.b: Faster. Your leg muscles use energy faster, so they need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide. The heart and lungs speed up to match.

items.f: You walk for ten minutes in the strong midday sun. What happens to your pulse?
items.b: Faster. The heart pumps extra blood to the skin to let heat out, as well as to the working muscles.

items.f: You have a fever and your temperature is 39 degrees Celsius. What happens to your pulse?
items.b: Faster. A warm body has cells that work faster, and the heart speeds up too. The pulse rises by about 10 beats for each degree of fever.

items.f: You breathe in slowly for four counts and out slowly for six counts, for two minutes. What happens?
items.b: Slower. Slow breathing sends calm signals to the heart, and the pulse often slows a little.

items.f: You watch the last over of a close cricket match. What happens to your pulse?
items.b: Faster. Excitement releases adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and harder even when you sit still.

items.f: You climb three floors of stairs. What happens to your pulse and breathing?
items.b: Faster. Climbing uses your big leg muscles hard, so they ask for more oxygen.

items.f: A runner who trains every day sits next to you, both at rest. How does her pulse compare with yours?
items.b: Slower. A trained heart pushes out more blood with each beat, so it does not have to beat as often.

items.f: A loud bang makes you jump. What happens to your pulse?
items.b: Faster. A fright releases adrenaline in seconds, and the heart speeds up even though you have not moved.

items.f: You sit wrapped in a blanket in a cold room. What happens to your pulse, compared with your resting rate?
items.b: About the same. In the cold, the vessels near the skin narrow, but the pulse changes little for a body that is resting.

items.f: You hold your breath for 20 seconds and then breathe again. What happens to your breathing rate right after?
items.b: Faster. Carbon dioxide builds up while you hold your breath, and the body breathes faster to clear it.

items.f: You skip with a rope for two minutes. What happens to your pulse and breathing?
items.b: Faster. Skipping works your whole body, and your muscles ask for oxygen.

items.f: You hold your breath with your face in a bowl of cold water. What happens to your pulse?
items.b: Slower. People have a diving reflex. Cold water on the face and a held breath slow the heart a little, which saves oxygen.

items.f: You have a half-hour nap on a hot afternoon. What happens to your pulse and breathing?
items.b: Slower. As you drift into sleep, your body needs less, and the pulse and breathing fall below the resting rate.

items.f: You are standing in a long queue at a shop. What happens, compared with your resting rate?
items.b: About the same. Standing quietly asks for a little more than sitting, but your pulse is close to your resting rate.

items.f: A visitor from Chennai arrives in Leh, at 3,500 metres, and sits down. What happens to her pulse and breathing?
items.b: Faster. Each breath has about one third less oxygen, so she breathes faster and her heart beats faster, even at rest.

items.f: You dance for ten minutes at a wedding. What happens to your pulse and breathing?
items.b: Faster. Dancing is exercise. Your muscles work hard and ask for more oxygen.

items.f: A young baby lies in a cot. How does the baby's pulse compare with yours?
items.b: Faster. A baby's heart is tiny and beats about 100 to 160 times a minute, much more than a school child's.

items.f: You sit in a waiting room, worrying about an injection. What happens to your pulse?
items.b: Faster. Worry releases a little adrenaline, and the heart speeds up even though your body is still.

items.f: You sit quietly for five minutes after a run that stopped five minutes ago. What happens, compared with right after you stopped?
items.b: Slower. The extra carbon dioxide has cleared, and the pulse and breathing have come back down to near rest.

items.f: You drink a glass of water while sitting. What happens to your pulse and breathing?
items.b: About the same. A glass of water asks almost nothing of the heart and lungs.

items.f: You swim ten laps in a pool. What happens to your pulse and breathing?
items.b: Faster. Swimming works the arms, legs and the whole body, so the muscles ask for more oxygen.

printables.title: 12 verdict tokens: four sets of three

rules: Faster, about the same and slower mean compared with your usual resting pulse and breathing, unless the card says otherwise.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front out loud, but not the back.
Everyone else picks one token and puts it face down. When the reader says now, everyone turns it over.
The reader then reads the back. Each player with the right token scores one point.
After each card, the reader asks one player to say, in their own words, what the cells are asking for. Then the reader role passes to the left.
Playing alone, put your token down, read the back, and score yourself. Try to beat your last score out of 24.
The game ends when the cards run out. The player with the most points wins. Everyone shares the best reason they heard.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 12 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards show situations in daily life. For each one, you decide whether your pulse and breathing go faster, stay about the same, or go slower. Get your tokens ready.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take one of each token.
flow.context: This is the first step of the card game. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: The tokens are Faster, About the same and Slower. Four sets of three are enough for four players. Alone, use one set. The game needs only paper, scissors and a pen; draw the three words on 12 small squares if you cannot print. A younger child can play with a parent as the reader.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. After each one, read the back aloud and ask what the cells are asking for.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone chooses a token and puts it face down. Turn them over together. Then read the back.
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.
flow.context: In this step you play the first eight cards and learn how to guess.

ask.q: What do your cells need more of when the pulse goes faster?
good: They need to get rid of carbon dioxide.

flow.parent: Do not tell the answers early. Let children argue. A child who guesses wrong and hears the reason is learning something.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards in the same way. Keep score. Ask one child to explain a reason in their own words.
flow.say: Keep going. After each card, one player explains why in their own words. Keep your score.
flow.kid: Play the next eight cards. Keep score. Explain one reason in your own words.
flow.context: In this step you play the next eight cards and explain reasons.
flow.think: Which cards were hardest to guess, and what did you learn from them?

flow.do: Play the last eight cards. Add up the scores. Talk about the cards that were hardest.
flow.say: Last eight cards. Then we count the scores. Which cards surprised you?
flow.kid: Play the last eight cards. Add up your score. Which cards surprised you?
flow.context: In this step you finish the game and look back at what surprised you.

check.q: Many cards said faster when the muscles were busy. What do all those cards have in common?
options: The cells were asking for more oxygen
The person was standing
The person was hot
check.why: Whenever cells use more energy, they need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide. The heart and lungs speed up to meet this. If you picked another answer, look at the cards about fright and fever, where the cause was different but the cells' demand was still higher.

projects.title: The Family Pulse Study: a pulse for every age

materials.item: a phone or kitchen clock with a stopwatch
a notebook, a pencil and a ruler
plain or squared paper for a bar chart
at least five family members or neighbours of different ages, who agree to join (a baby, a toddler or a grandparent is a bonus, but any five ages will do; ask on a phone call if needed)

projects.safety: Ask each person first. Count only people who are sitting quietly. Count a baby's heartbeat with a flat hand on the chest, and do not wake a sleeping baby.

schedule.what: Ask each person to sit still for two minutes. Count each pulse for 15 seconds twice, and use the average. Multiply by 4. Write the age and the pulse.
Draw a bar chart of pulse against age. Write what you see. Write one thing you cannot tell from five people.

projects.record: Write each person's age and pulse per minute. Draw a bar chart. Write one sentence on the pattern you see and one sentence on what the study cannot tell you.
projects.context: In this project you measure the resting pulse of at least five people of different ages, and make a bar chart. You find out whether children, parents and grandparents have different pulses.

setup.art: A child counting a grandmother's pulse at her wrist while they both sit on a sofa, with a stopwatch on the table.
setup.caption: 1. Ask a person to sit quietly for two minutes. Count their pulse for 15 seconds.

setup.art: A notebook table with five names, ages, counts and the multiply by 4 results.
setup.caption: 2. Write the age and the pulse per minute for each person.

setup.art: A bar chart with age labels along the bottom and bars of different heights.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar chart. Look for a pattern.

flow.do: Ask the child to guess whether older or younger people have the faster resting pulse, and why. Write the guess. Choose five or more people of different ages.
flow.say: Do you think older people or younger people have a faster pulse at rest? Why do you think so? Choose five people to count.
flow.kid: Who has the faster pulse, old or young people? Why? Choose five people.
flow.context: In this step you guess and choose the people to count.
flow.parent: Include a baby or toddler if you can, a child, a parent, and a grandparent. Count all of them at the same time of day, if possible.

flow.do: Ask each person to sit still for two minutes. Count each pulse for 15 seconds, wait a minute, and count again. Add the two counts and multiply by 2 to get beats per minute. Write the age and the pulse.
flow.say: Ask each person to sit quietly for two minutes. Then count their pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4.
flow.kid: Ask each person to sit still. Count the pulse for 15 seconds. Multiply by 4.
flow.context: In this step you measure the resting pulse of each person.
flow.parent: Usual resting rates are about 100 to 160 for a newborn, 70 to 110 for a school child, and 60 to 100 for an adult. A person who exercises regularly may be below 60. With 2 to 4 children, share the people out, with each child counting their own people while a sibling times; swap for one person to check that two counters agree. A person can count their own pulse while the child times. Use the same time of day for all, and do not count anyone who has just run or eaten a big meal.

check.q: You counted 18 beats in 15 seconds for a grandfather. What is his pulse per minute?
check.why: 18 times 4 is 72. If you picked 33, you added 15. Multiplying by 4 gives beats in a full minute.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart with the ages along the bottom and the pulse per minute going up. Write what you see. Write one thing you cannot tell from only five people.
flow.say: Draw a bar for each person. Look at the pattern. Does age change the pulse? What could you not tell from only five people?
flow.kid: Draw a bar chart. Write the pattern you see. Write what five people cannot tell you.
flow.context: In this step you draw a bar chart and say what it shows.

ask.q: What is one thing five people cannot tell us?
good: Whether it is true for everyone.

flow.parent: Five people are too few to be sure of a pattern. A good scientist says so. Fit people often have a lower pulse, whatever their age, so a fit grandparent may break the pattern.
flow.think: Which person in your family might have the lowest resting pulse, and why?

challenges.title: The Tummy Lever: count breaths without anyone noticing
challenges.problem: When people know their breaths are being counted, they change how they breathe. Design a breath-meter that shows each breath without anyone watching the chest, so you can count a sleeping person's breathing.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
The meter must sit on the belly of a person lying still on their back.
It must show each breath so clearly that you can count from a distance.
It must be light, so it does not make breathing hard.
A grown-up must be beside the person being measured.
materials: a lump of clay or dough
general: Place a light paper cup upside down on the belly. Watch it rise and fall as the person breathes.
Stand a small paper flag on the belly and watch it tilt and straighten with each breath.
Put a light book on the belly and watch it lift. Count each lift.
creative: Make a lever with the straw. Press a lump of clay on a stack of books so that a straw pivots on it. Rest the short end on the cup on the belly. The long end moves up and down about five times as far as the belly moves.
Tape a bright paper arrow to the long end of the lever, and mark a card behind it. Count each time the arrow crosses the line.
Use a lever with a paper pointer and mark a strip for the highest and lowest points, to see how deep each breath is as well as how many there are.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own breath-meter. Test it on a resting person for one minute, and compare its count with a count made by watching the belly. Which is more accurate, and which is easier to read from across the room?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about counting breaths. You build a meter that makes each breath easy to see without the person noticing.

setup.art: A person lying on their back with a paper cup on their belly and a straw lever resting on it, with a pencil and clay pivot beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Rest a paper cup on the belly and balance a straw lever on a clay pivot.

setup.art: A close-up of the straw lever with a long end moving up and down with a bright paper flag.
setup.caption: 2. Watch the long end of the lever move with each breath.

setup.art: A notebook with a tally of marks for one minute and the number 18 circled.
setup.caption: 3. Count the movements for one minute with a stopwatch.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask why counting a breath changes it. Ask the child to suggest ways to see a breath from a distance.
flow.say: When people know their breaths are being counted, they breathe differently. How could you count breaths without a person noticing?
flow.kid: Counting breaths changes breathing. How could you count without anyone noticing?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tummy Lever challenge. You think about the problem.

ask.q: What moves when a person breathes?

flow.do: Place the cup on the belly of a person lying still on their back. Build the lever. Press clay onto a stack of books. Push the straw into the clay, a quarter of the way along. Rest the short end on the cup. Check that the long end moves.
flow.say: Lie on your back, with a paper cup on your belly. We will balance a straw on a lump of clay with its short end on the cup. Breathe naturally.
flow.kid: Put a cup on your belly. Balance a straw so its short end rests on the cup.
flow.context: In this step you build the lever and place it on the belly.
flow.parent: The straw is a lever. The short side moves a little, and the long side moves a lot. If the straw does not move, move the clay closer to the cup. If the cup tips, use a lighter cup.

flow.do: Count the movements of the long end of the straw for one minute. Then count the belly by watching it for one minute. Write both numbers down.
flow.say: Count the lifts of the long end of the straw for one minute. Then we compare it with a count made by watching the belly.
flow.kid: Count the lifts for one minute. Compare with a count made by watching.
flow.context: In this step you test your breath-meter against a plain count.
flow.think: What would you change to make your meter more exact?

check.q: Why is the long end of the lever easier to count than the belly?
options: It moves further than the belly does
It moves faster than the belly
It is lighter than the belly
check.why: A lever makes a small movement into a large one. The short side moves a little and the long side moves five times as far, so it is easier to see. If you picked another answer, measure how far each end moves with a ruler.

items.p: A child's pulse is counted for 15 seconds, and the count is 22 beats. What is the pulse per minute?
items.why: There are four 15-second spells in one minute. 22 times 4 is 88. If you chose 37, you added 15 to the count instead of multiplying.

items.p: One breath is one time in and one time ____.
a: out
items.why: A breath has two halves, in and out. When you count breaths, count each full in-and-out as one.

items.p: A child who is sitting still usually has a pulse of about 70 to 110 beats per minute.
items.why: True. Children aged 6 to 10 usually have a resting pulse in this range. Grown-ups are usually slower, and babies are faster.

items.p: What do red blood cells carry from the lungs to the cells of the body?
items.why: Red blood cells pick up oxygen in the lungs and let go of it in the tissues. Carbon dioxide travels the other way, mostly dissolved in the plasma.

items.p: Cells use food to get energy. What gas do they make as waste?
items.why: Cells use oxygen to release energy from sugar, and they give out carbon dioxide and water. The carbon dioxide travels in the blood back to the lungs.

items.p: Match each part of the blood to its job.
pairs: the pale liquid that carries cells and food
the red protein that holds oxygen
items.why: Blood is a mix of liquid and different cells, and each one has its own job.

items.p: Red blood cells are red because they are full of a red protein with iron in it, called ____.
a: haemoglobin
hemoglobin
items.why: Haemoglobin holds oxygen. It has iron at its centre, which is why the body needs iron in food.

items.p: Which blood vessels are so thin that red blood cells pass through them in single file?
items.why: A capillary is only one cell thick, and it is narrow enough that red cells must go through one at a time. This lets oxygen cross easily into the cells around it.

items.p: Put these in order, to follow one oxygen molecule from the air to a muscle cell.
items: It crosses the thin wall of an alveolus into a capillary
It is breathed in through the nose
It is pumped out of the heart to the leg muscle
It travels down the windpipe to the lungs
It is carried to the heart by a red blood cell
a: It is breathed in through the nose
It travels down the windpipe to the lungs
It crosses the thin wall of an alveolus into a capillary
It is carried to the heart by a red blood cell
It is pumped out of the heart to the leg muscle
items.why: Oxygen goes from the nose to the lungs, across into the blood, along to the heart, and out to the muscle.

items.p: Blood in your veins is blue until it touches the air.
items.why: False. Blood is always red. It is bright red with oxygen and dark red without much. Veins look blue because of the way light goes through skin.

items.p: Your pulse and your breathing both go up when you run. What is the best reason?
opts: Your muscle cells need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide
Your heart and lungs are tired
Your brain wants to cool the blood
items.why: Busy muscles use oxygen faster and make more carbon dioxide. The heart and lungs speed up to deliver the oxygen and clear the carbon dioxide.

items.p: Is each job done by the right side or the left side of the heart?
items: sends blood to the whole body
receives blood coming back from the body
receives blood coming back from the lungs
items.why: The right side sends blood a short way to the lungs. The left side sends it all the way round the body, so it needs the thicker wall.

items.p: Here is a picture of the heart cut open. Label the four rooms: top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right, as you look at the picture.
a: Top left of the picture: right atrium
Top right of the picture: left atrium
Bottom left of the picture: right ventricle
Bottom right of the picture: left ventricle
items.why: In pictures, the heart is drawn as if you face the person, so the person's right side is on the left of the picture.
items.art: A heart cut open showing four rooms, with an empty label box next to each room.

items.p: A friend says: 'You breathe faster when you run because you run out of oxygen.' What can you tell her, using what you found out?
items.a: Breathing speeds up mainly because carbon dioxide builds up in the blood when muscles work. Sensors notice the carbon dioxide and tell the lungs to breathe faster, and the heart speeds up to match. Oxygen does not run out.
items.why: A strong answer names carbon dioxide as the main signal and says that the heart and lungs answer what the cells are doing.

items.p: Draw the heart as two pumps side by side. Show an arrow from the right pump to the lungs, and an arrow from the left pump to the body, and one arrow back to each.
items.a: Two pumps side by side. An arrow goes from the right one to the lungs and back to the left one. An arrow goes from the left one to the body and back to the right one.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two loops that meet at the heart, so blood goes through the heart twice on one full trip.
items.art: A blank box with two circles in the middle for the pumps, a lung drawn on the left and a body drawn on the right.

items.p: A child's heart beats 80 times a minute. How many times does it beat in 10 minutes?
items.why: 80 times 10 is 800. Multiplying by 10 puts a zero on the end.

items.p: You press a fingernail until it goes white, and the pink comes back slowly. What does this suggest?
opts: Less blood is reaching the fingertip
The finger has too much blood
items.why: A white nail is a nail with the blood squeezed out. The pink returns when new blood arrives. If it comes back slowly, the blood is arriving slowly, as in cold fingers.

items.p: Your lungs have hundreds of millions of tiny air bags and not one big bag. Why does this help?
opts: It gives a huge surface for oxygen to cross into the blood
items.why: Oxygen crosses the lung's thin wall, and the more wall there is, the more oxygen can cross each second. Many small bags have more surface than one big bag of the same volume.

items.p: A crushed sugar lump dissolves faster than a whole one. What does this tell you about why lungs fold into so many bags?
opts: More surface means a faster swap
Warm water is better for powder
items.why: A swap happens only where two things touch. Breaking something into many small pieces gives much more touching surface.

items.p: The air you breathe out has no oxygen left in it.
items.why: False. Breathed-out air still holds about 16 parts oxygen in 100. The body takes only about a quarter of the oxygen in each breath.

items.p: The level of ____ in the blood is the main signal that tells your body to breathe faster.
a: carbon dioxide
items.why: Sensors in the brainstem and in the big arteries of the neck notice carbon dioxide rising, and tell the breathing muscles to work harder.

items.p: Your pulse is a few beats higher when you stand than when you lie down. What is the likely reason?
opts: Gravity pulls blood to the legs, so the heart speeds up to keep it reaching the brain
The wrist moves nearer the heart
items.why: When you stand, blood tends to pool in the legs. The heart beats a little faster to keep blood moving to the head.

items.p: Put these in order, from the slowest resting heart to the fastest.
a: an elephant
a person
a mouse
items.why: An elephant's heart beats about 30 times a minute, a person's about 70, and a mouse's about 600. Smaller bodies use energy faster for their size, so their hearts beat faster.

items.p: A tube of blood has settled into three layers. Label them from the top to the bottom.
a: Top: plasma
Middle, a thin layer: white blood cells and platelets
Bottom: red blood cells
items.why: Plasma is the lightest part and floats on top. The red cells are the heaviest and sink to the bottom. The thin pale layer in between holds the white cells and the platelets.
items.art: A tall test tube with a yellow top layer, a thin white layer and a thick red layer, and empty label boxes beside them.

items.p: Why might a person with anaemia get out of breath sooner on the stairs than a person without it?
items.a: A person with anaemia has fewer red blood cells or less haemoglobin, so each beat of the heart carries less oxygen to the muscles. On the stairs, the muscles ask for more oxygen, so the body breathes faster and the heart beats faster sooner.
items.why: A strong answer links fewer red cells to less oxygen delivered, and so to the body having to work harder to deliver enough.

items.p: After a month in Leh, a visitor feels much better on the stairs. What has changed in her body?
opts: She has more red blood cells to carry oxygen
items.why: In thin air, the body makes more red blood cells over weeks, so each pass of the blood carries more oxygen.

items.p: Match each living being to the way it moves oxygen round its body.
pairs: a heart that beats about 600 times a minute
three hearts and blood with copper
a heart with two rooms and one loop
air tubes that go straight into the body
a heart with four rooms and two loops
items.why: Moving oxygen is a problem every body must solve, and living things have solved it in different ways.

items.p: Two children are arguing about what makes the heart speed up when you run.

views.who: Devika, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The heart is the boss of the body. It decides how fast to go, and everything else follows.

views.who: Karthik, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The heart answers the muscles. When they use more oxygen, they send signals, and the heart speeds up to match.

views.who: Dr Nandini, a heart doctor (an imagined view)
views.says: The heart has its own built-in pacemaker, but nerves and hormones speed it up or slow it down. So both children have a point.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from the Pulse Detective test. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer uses the test, for example that the pulse and breathing rose together and fell together, which suggests they answer the same call. It also admits that the heart has a built-in pacemaker.
items.why: The heart does have its own rhythm, and signals from outside change it. Seeing both sides is better than picking only one.

items.p: Why does the left side of the heart have a thicker wall than the right?
opts: It pushes blood all the way round the body
It is bigger than the right
It is older than the right
items.why: The right side sends blood a short way to the lungs. The left side must push blood through the whole body, so it needs stronger muscle.

items.p: A child's heart pushes out 45 millilitres of blood with each beat, and beats 80 times in a minute. How many millilitres of blood is that in one minute?
items.why: 45 times 80 is 3,600. That is 3.6 litres, more than the 2 to 3 litres of blood in the child's whole body. So the same blood must go round more than once each minute.

items.p: Veins have small flaps inside that stop blood from slipping backwards.
items.why: True. The flaps act as one-way doors. When leg muscles squeeze the veins, blood is pushed up towards the heart, and the flaps stop it from falling back.

items.p: In the Cold Fingers test, the pink came back in 1 second in a warm hand and in 4 seconds in a cold hand. Write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
items.a: Claim: blood reaches the fingertips more slowly when they are cold. Evidence: the pink took 1 second in the warm hand and 4 seconds in the cold hand. Reasoning: in the cold, the small vessels near the skin narrow, so less blood arrives, which keeps the middle of the body warm.
items.why: A strong answer has all three parts, uses the numbers as evidence, and links them to narrow vessels.

items.p: In each situation, do the small blood vessels near the skin get narrower or wider?
items: standing outside on a cold morning
dipping a hand in ice water
items.why: In the cold, the body saves heat by narrowing the vessels near the skin. In the heat, it widens them to let heat out.

items.p: A friend counts 14 beats in 10 seconds. What is her pulse per minute?
items.why: There are six 10-second spells in one minute. 14 times 6 is 84. If you chose 140, you multiplied by 10 instead of 6.

items.p: After exercise, a child's pulse falls from 150 to 90 beats per minute in 3 minutes, falling by the same amount each minute. By how many beats per minute does it fall each minute?
items.why: 150 take away 90 is 60. 60 divided by 3 is 20. So the pulse fell by 20 beats per minute, each minute.

items.p: Some people breathe fast and deep many times and then hold their breath, and a few faint. What explains this?
opts: Fast breathing removes carbon dioxide, so the urge to breathe goes away while oxygen is still falling
Fast breathing adds too much oxygen
Holding the breath makes blood too thin
items.why: The urge to breathe is set by carbon dioxide, not by oxygen. If you wash out the carbon dioxide first, the warning comes late, and oxygen can fall too low. This is dangerous, so never do it, especially in water.

items.p: Three of these make the heart beat faster. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Fright, fever and climbing all raise the pulse. Deep sleep slows it.

items.p: A mouse's heart beats about 600 times a minute and an elephant's about 30. Using the idea of cells that need oxygen, explain one reason for the difference.
items.a: A small body loses heat fast and each gram of a mouse uses oxygen much faster than a gram of an elephant. So a mouse's cells ask for oxygen at a faster rate, and the heart must deliver faster.
items.why: A strong answer links the heart rate to how quickly the cells use oxygen, which depends on the size of the body.

items.p: An octopus has blue-green blood. What is the reason?
opts: It carries oxygen with copper instead of iron
It has no oxygen in it
items.why: The octopus's oxygen carrier has copper, and copper makes the blood bluish. Ours has iron, and iron makes blood red.

items.p: In a tree, sugar and water are moved round by a heart.
items.why: False. A tree has no heart. Water is pulled up by the loss of water from the leaves, and sugar moves down tubes from the leaves to the rest of the tree.

items.p: People have long said that feelings live in the heart.

views.says: When I am frightened or in love, I can feel my heart race. So feelings live in the heart.
Feelings are felt in the heart because the brain sends signals to it. If the brain is hurt, feelings change. If the heart is replaced, the person stays the same.
The heart and brain are in constant conversation, and the heart has its own nerve cells. We may be wrong to say all feeling stays in one place.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say one thing the others have right.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer uses evidence, such as the heart-transplant fact or the racing heart in fear, and admits that each view has a point.
items.why: Racing hearts are real, and brain damage changing feelings is real too. The question of where feelings live is still open.

items.p: Why do climbers rest for days partway up a high mountain before going higher?
opts: The body needs time to make more red blood cells and adjust its breathing
The food is better at the lower camps
The air is warmer at the lower camps
items.why: It takes days to weeks for the body to adjust to thin air. Going too fast can cause altitude sickness.

items.p: Match each tool to what it tells a doctor.
pairs: lets the doctor listen to the heart and lungs
shows how much of the haemoglobin is carrying oxygen
shows how much haemoglobin is in the blood
measures how much air a person can breathe out
items.why: Each tool lets us see a different part of what the heart, blood and lungs are doing.

items.p: A child's pulse after exercise was 138 at 0 minutes, 112 at 1 minute, 98 at 2 minutes, 90 at 3 minutes and 86 at 4 minutes. Draw a line graph of these.
items.a: A graph with minutes along the bottom from 0 to 4 and pulse up the side. The line starts high at 138 and drops steeply, then flattens out near 86.
items.why: A line graph shows the fall in pulse and how it slows down. The steepest fall is in the first minute.
items.art: A blank graph with minutes along the bottom and beats per minute up the side.

items.p: A pulse oximeter clipped to a finger shows 98 percent. What does this mean?
opts: About 98 out of every 100 haemoglobin molecules are carrying oxygen
98 percent of the air is oxygen
The pulse is 98 beats a minute
items.why: A pulse oximeter shines light through the finger and measures how much of the haemoglobin is holding oxygen. It often shows the pulse in a separate number.

items.p: Plan a fair test of this question: do children who play sport every day recover their pulse faster than children who do not? Say what you would keep the same.
items.a: Test several children from each group. Have each do the same one minute of step-ups on the same step, and count the pulse every minute for four minutes. Keep the exercise, the counting, the time of day and the way of counting the same. Compare the time to return close to resting.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, the sport habit, and keeps the rest the same, and uses more than one child from each group.

items.p: A red blood cell lives for about 120 days. About how many weeks is that, to the nearest whole week?
items.why: 120 divided by 7 is about 17.1. So a red blood cell lives about 17 weeks, a little over four months.

items.p: At 3,500 metres, each breath holds about two thirds as much oxygen as at sea level. Which could help the body get the same oxygen?
opts: Breathing faster, pumping more blood and making more red blood cells
items.why: All three of the first list help: more breaths bring in more air, more pumping moves it faster, and more red cells carry more per trip.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how your body answers when you start to run.
items: The breathing and the pulse speed up
Muscle cells use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide
More oxygen reaches the muscle cells
Sensors notice the carbon dioxide rising
a: Muscle cells use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide
Sensors notice the carbon dioxide rising
The breathing and the pulse speed up
More oxygen reaches the muscle cells
items.why: The cells call first. The sensors notice. The lungs and heart speed up. More oxygen is delivered, which meets the cells' call.

quiz.p: You count 25 beats in 15 seconds. What is the pulse per minute?
quiz.why: There are four 15-second spells in a minute. 25 times 4 is 100. If you chose 40, you added 15.

quiz.p: Why is it better if the person does not know you are counting their breaths?
opts: People change how they breathe when they know it is being counted
The count is easier to do
quiz.why: When we notice our breathing, we often change it. A fair count should be of normal breathing.

quiz.p: What does the blood bring to a muscle cell?
quiz.why: Blood brings both sugar from food and oxygen. The cell uses them together to release energy.

opts: Haemoglobin, a red protein with iron in it
quiz.why: Haemoglobin holds oxygen and is red. Blood is red whether or not the person has just breathed.

quiz.p: Which part of the heart pushes blood to the whole body?
opts: Both sides do the same job
quiz.why: The right side sends blood to the lungs and the left side sends it to the whole body.

quiz.p: Why are the walls of the alveoli so thin?
opts: So oxygen can pass through quickly into the blood
quiz.why: A swap needs a thin wall. Oxygen crosses a wall that is only half a thousandth of a millimetre thick.

quiz.p: Which gas level in the blood mostly tells your body to breathe faster?
quiz.why: Rising carbon dioxide is the main signal. Falling oxygen matters later and only when it falls a long way.

quiz.p: Hana's fingers are white and cold after a swim. When she presses a nail, the pink returns slowly. What is her body doing?
opts: Sending less blood to the fingers to keep the middle of the body warm
Making more blood in the fingers
quiz.why: In the cold, the small vessels near the skin narrow. The blood stays near the heart and the other organs that must stay warm.

quiz.p: Which of these would give the lowest pulse?
quiz.why: During deep sleep the cells need less energy, so the pulse falls below the usual resting rate.

quiz.p: A child counts her pulse three times and gets 80, 84 and 82. What does this show?
opts: The count is steady, so we can trust it
quiz.why: Results that are close together show that the test gives about the same answer each time. A few beats of difference is normal.

quiz.p: Why does a visitor to Leh breathe faster at first?
opts: Each breath of thin air holds less oxygen
quiz.why: At 3,500 metres the air has about two thirds of the oxygen per breath. Breathing faster brings in more air.

quiz.p: A nurse takes blood from a vein in your arm. What colour is the blood in the syringe?
quiz.why: Blood is always red. Blood from a vein has given up some oxygen, so it is dark red.

maths.problem: In the Pulse Detective test, Kavya counted 21 beats in 15 seconds lying down and 33 beats in 15 seconds just after step-ups. What was her pulse per minute each time? How many more beats per minute was it after the step-ups?
maths.answer: 84 and 132. It was 48 beats per minute more.
maths.explain: 21 times 4 is 84. 33 times 4 is 132. 132 take away 84 is 48.
maths.context: In the Pulse Detective test, you count the pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. These are made-up counts for a child called Kavya.
maths.why_maths: A 15-second count must be multiplied by 4 to compare with the pulse per minute. Subtracting then shows how big the change was.

maths.problem: Kavya's pulse at rest was 84 beats per minute, and she breathed 21 times a minute. About how many heartbeats are there for each breath?
maths.explain: 84 divided by 21 is 4. So there are 4 heartbeats for each breath.
maths.context: In the Pulse Detective test, you count pulse and breaths for the same minute. These are made-up results for a child called Kavya.
maths.why_maths: A ratio shows how two counts go together. In this test the ratio stays close to the same even when both numbers change.

maths.problem: Look at the line graph of a child's pulse after step-ups. At what minute was the pulse first within 10 beats of the resting pulse of 84? How many beats did it fall in the first minute?
maths.answer: At 3 minutes (pulse 90). It fell by 26 beats in the first minute.
maths.explain: Within 10 of 84 means 94 or lower. At 2 minutes it was 100. At 3 minutes it was 90, which is within 10. In the first minute it fell from 138 to 112. 138 take away 112 is 26.
maths.context: In the Pulse Detective test, you count the pulse every minute after exercise and draw a line graph. This graph shows made-up results.

chart.title: Pulse after one minute of step-ups

maths.why_maths: A line graph shows how fast the pulse comes down, and where it flattens. Reading it tells us how long a body takes to settle.

maths.problem: A child's resting pulse is 84 beats per minute. How many times does the heart beat in one whole day? One day has 24 hours, and each hour has 60 minutes.
maths.explain: 24 times 60 is 1,440 minutes in a day. 84 times 1,440 is 120,960.
maths.why_maths: Your pulse is a small number every minute, but it never stops. Multiplying shows how many times the heart works in a day.

maths.problem: About 2 million new red blood cells are made in an adult's bone marrow every second. About how many are made in one hour? One hour has 3,600 seconds.
maths.answer: 7,200,000,000 red blood cells, which is 7.2 billion.
maths.explain: 2 million times 3,600 is 7,200 million, which is 7,200,000,000.
maths.why_maths: Red blood cells live only about four months, so the body must keep making them. Big numbers show how busy the bone marrow is.

maths.problem: A classroom floor is 8 metres long and 6 metres wide. The surface of an adult's lungs is about 60 square metres. How many square metres bigger than the floor is the lung surface?
maths.explain: The floor area is 8 times 6, which is 48 square metres. 60 take away 48 is 12.
maths.context: In the Big Surface test, you saw that more surface means a faster swap. The lungs fold up their surface to fit inside a chest. The lung surface of 60 square metres is a middle value of an estimate that ranges from 50 to 100.
maths.why_maths: Area tells us how much surface there is. Comparing it with a room we know makes the huge lung surface easier to picture.

maths.problem: In the Big Surface test, a made-up sugar lump took 12 minutes to dissolve whole, 3 minutes crushed and 1 minute as a powder. How many times faster was the crushed sugar than the lump? How many times faster was the powder?
maths.answer: The crushed sugar was 4 times faster. The powder was 12 times faster.
maths.explain: 12 divided by 3 is 4. 12 divided by 1 is 12.
maths.context: In the Big Surface test, you dissolve the same sugar as a lump, in crushed bits and as a powder. These are made-up times.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the two times says how many times faster one is. It tells us how much the extra surface helped.

maths.problem: Look at the bar chart of breaths per minute. How many more breaths per minute does the baby take than the grown-up? How many times as many breaths does the baby take as the child?
maths.answer: 24 more breaths. The baby breathes 2 times as often as the child.
maths.explain: The baby is at 40 and the grown-up is at 16. 40 take away 16 is 24. The child is at 20. 40 divided by 20 is 2.
maths.context: In the breath count of the family, you count breaths in 15 seconds for each being and draw a bar chart. This chart shows made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance who breathes fastest. The difference between two bars tells how much faster.

maths.problem: Estimate how many times a heart beats in a life of 80 years at 70 beats per minute. Round: 70 times 60 is 4,200 an hour, and one day is about 100,000 beats. A year is about 365 days.
maths.answer: About 2.9 billion beats, so about 3 billion.
maths.explain: 100,000 beats a day times 365 days is about 36,500,000 beats a year. 36,500,000 times 80 years is about 2,920,000,000, which is about 3 billion.
maths.why_maths: A heart beats so often that the exact total hardly matters. Rounding quickly gives a number we can think about.

applications: Doctors count the pulse and breathing rate of every patient, because the two numbers show quickly how the body is coping.
A pulse oximeter clipped to a finger shows how much of the blood's haemoglobin is carrying oxygen.
A stethoscope lets a doctor hear the valves of the heart close and the air moving in the lungs.
Blood tests count red blood cells and haemoglobin, to find anaemia.
Giving iron tablets and iron-rich food, such as ragi, jaggery, dal and green leaves, helps to treat anaemia.
Athletes watch their resting pulse and their recovery pulse to see how fit they are.
Mountaineers rest on the way up so their bodies can make more red blood cells.
Heart-lung machines do the work of the heart and lungs for a few hours during heart surgery.
A face mask with extra oxygen helps people who find it hard to breathe.
Exercise, such as skipping, swimming and playing kabaddi, makes the heart stronger.

open_questions.q: Why does the heart of each animal beat at the speed they do, and is there a limit to the number of beats in a life?
open_questions.why_open: Small animals have fast hearts and short lives, but people live much longer than the pattern predicts, so no one has a firm rule.

open_questions.q: How do heart cells that start beating on their own in a dish learn to beat together in time?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that cells signal each other through tiny channels, but they are still working out the full detail.

open_questions.q: Why do some people adapt well to life at high altitude and others do not?
open_questions.why_open: Gene changes are known in Tibetans and Andeans, but many other factors are not understood.

open_questions.q: How much does breathing slowly and deeply really change the heart, the brain and the mood?
open_questions.why_open: Studies often find small benefits, but they are hard to run well, and the results are mixed.

open_questions.q: How exactly do the body's sensors measure oxygen and carbon dioxide so quickly?
open_questions.why_open: Cells in the neck's carotid bodies are known to be sensors, but the exact detail of how they sense oxygen is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why are so many women and children in India anaemic, even with food available?
open_questions.why_open: Poor diet, infections, blood loss and long-standing patterns of who eats first all play a part, and researchers are still working out how much each one matters.

roots.context: We have counted our pulse and breath, followed oxygen to the cells, and seen how blood goes where it is needed. Now we ask what this tells us about who is in charge of a body, and what we are made of.

deep_truth.truth: Your heart is not the boss of your body. It speeds up because your cells ask for more oxygen, and your lungs speed up for the same reason. Pulse, breath and blood together make one answer to millions of small requests.
deep_truth.habit: We picture the heart as an engine or a boss that sets the pace, and the lungs as a separate pair of bellows. This splits one job into separate machines. In the test, the pulse and the breathing rose and fell together, because both were answering the same call from the cells.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Pulse Detective test, the pulse and the breathing rate both rose after the step-ups and both came back down together over about four minutes. Muscle cells were using more oxygen and making more carbon dioxide, and carbon dioxide in the blood is the signal that speeds up both.

three.who_am_i: You are not one thing in charge of the rest. You are trillions of cells, each asking for what it needs, with a heart and lungs that answer.
three.what_is_life: Life is a constant exchange. Oxygen comes in, carbon dioxide goes out, and the flow does not stop for even a minute.
three.what_is_this_world: The oxygen in your blood was made by plants, algae and microbes. The iron in your blood was made inside stars, long before the Sun.

roots.thread: A few weeks after you began, a tiny tube of heart cells started to beat, long before there was a brain to give orders. A heart cell can even beat alone in a dish, and cells placed together soon beat in time. In your body, trillions of cells ask for oxygen and send out carbon dioxide, and one heartbeat answers all of them. The heart, the lungs and the blood are not three machines. They are one process that shows up as many parts, the way the One shows up as the many.

teachings.teaching: The powers of the body, such as speech, mind, sight and hearing, each said that it was the chief one. Prana, the breath of life, began to leave, and all the others began to leave with it, like bees following a queen. They saw that they all depended on the breath.
teachings.link: The Upanishad picks the breath as the one that holds the rest together. In our science, the dependence goes both ways, because no cell works without oxygen and the breath and the heartbeat answer to the cells.

teachings.teaching: The true people of old breathed from their heels, and ordinary people breathe from their throats.
teachings.link: A slow, deep breath reaches further into the lungs than a quick, shallow one. At rest, the body asks for little, and the breath can be slow and deep.

teachings.source: Kabir, 'Student, tell me, what is God?' (15th century, in Robert Bly's translation)
teachings.teaching: Kabir answers: he is the breath inside the breath.
teachings.link: Each breath brings in air, but the oxygen is what matters. It crosses a wall half a thousandth of a millimetre thick and rides inside a red blood cell. There is a breath inside the breath.

science.text: Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by living things. About 2.4 billion years ago, bacteria in the sea began to use sunlight to split water, and the oxygen they gave out slowly filled the air.
The iron at the heart of haemoglobin was made inside stars and thrown out when they exploded. Every iron atom in your blood is older than the Sun.

other_view.view: Heart cells have a built-in pacemaker, and nerves and hormones only speed it up or slow it down. They describe the whole body as feedback loops of chemicals and signals, and do not say that cells ask for anything. Whether such a description is complete is a deep question.

how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, many people followed Aristotle, who taught that the heart is the hottest part of the body and that we breathe to cool it, like fanning a hot pot. In the 1770s, Joseph Priestley and Carl Scheele each found a new air that made flames burn bright. Antoine Lavoisier, in France, named it oxygen. Around 1783, he and Pierre Laplace put a guinea pig in a chamber packed with ice. The animal's warmth melted the ice, and they measured the carbon dioxide it breathed out. The heat for each bit of carbon dioxide was close to that of burning charcoal. So breathing was not cooling. It was a slow, gentle burning of food. In 1789 and 1790, Lavoisier tested a young man, Armand Seguin, breathing through a mask at rest and while lifting weights. Seguin used far more oxygen when he worked. Lavoisier's wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, took notes and drew the apparatus.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristotle, Joseph Priestley, Carl Scheele, Antoine Lavoisier, Pierre Laplace, Armand Seguin and Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier
how_we_found_out.when: Aristotle about 350 BCE, the discovery of oxygen in the 1770s, the ice experiment about 1783, and the human breathing tests in 1789 and 1790
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle taught that breathing cools the heart, and later thinkers said that air only carried away hot vapours. Lavoisier's ice and oxygen measurements showed that breathing is slow burning of food, which makes heat and carbon dioxide, and that working harder uses more oxygen.

playtest: Read as a parent and a child in a city flat would use it, but not yet done with a real child. The Pulse Detective needs only a step or a stair, a stopwatch and a notebook, and takes about 55 minutes. Counts over 15 seconds are rough, so tell the child the numbers can differ by a few beats. Counting breaths works best when the child does not know. For Cold Fingers, expect the pink to return in about a second in a warm hand and a few seconds in a cold one. If the times look alike, compare the colour of the fingertips. The cold part is one minute only. For Big Surface, the powder is quick, in under a minute, and a whole lump can take 10 minutes or more in warm water, so keep it unstirred. The cereal magnet may find nothing if the magnet is weak.
